title: Petrvm viaco
name_variants: Petrvm viaco@la | Petromantulum | Petrum Viaco | Petrvm viaco
details: The placename "Petromantalum" (or in some editions "Petromantulum") appears in the Antonine Itineraries on a route from " Caracotinum " to " Augustobona ", where it lies between " Ritumago " and " Luticiam " (modern Paris). Scholars have long identified this place as coincident with one "Petrum viaco", which appears on the Peutinger map after "Ritumagus" and is connected onward to both " Casaromago " and " Brivisara ". A number of modern locations have been suggested over the years for the site of this Petromant[a|u]lum/Petrum viaco . In compiling Map 11 for the Barrington Atlas, C. Haselgrove cites and follows (without comment) TIR Lutetia (published in 1975), which will go only so far as to say the site must be in the "région de Magny-en-Vexin (Val-d'Oise)". Several discussions of possible sites are summarized therein, including Guiry-en-Vexin (see Guiry-Gadancourt ), Radepont, St-Clair-sur-Epte, St-Gervais, and a site called Les Vaux-de-la-Celle at Genainville . J-M Desbordes, writing in the Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites (published in 1976), confidently associates Petromantalum with Les Vaux de la Celle , making no mention of other suggestions or of the rationale for the identification. Haselgrove does not seem to have shared this opinion, since he maps Genainville (incorrectly labeled Génainville) separately and cites PECS in neither context. Writing also in 1976 in the Journal des savants , M. Roblin argues at length for St-Clair-sur-Epte as the identification . This argument seems to have been accepted tentatively by at least some other scholars writing in the francophone tradition (but Elliott has not conducted a full survey of the literature). Rather than privileging one or another of these options here, we have left this place resource unlocated but added a connection and appropriate note to the existing place resource for Genainville (Le Vaux de la Celle).
description: An ancient settlement or road station, attested by both the Antonine Itineraries and the Peutinger Map, whose precise location is uncertain (BAtlas 11 unlocated Petromantulum/Petrum Viaco).

description: Alb(i)um Intimilium/Albintimilium (modern Ventimiglia) was the main settlement of the Ligurian tribe of the Intemelii. In the 2nd century BC, it came under the control of the Roman Republic. Albintimilium became a municipium in 89 BC in the tribus Falerna. In the same period, the city walls were built, with several towers. The city flourished in the early Imperial period, with baths, an aqueduct, and a theater. In the 6th and early 7th century, it was a Byzantine kastron, coming under the control of the Longobards in 641. During the 7th and 8th centuries, the Roman city was slowly abandoned in favour of a smaller hilltop settlement focused around the Cathedral.

title: Ad Herculem
name_variants: Ad Herculem@la | Ad Herculem
details: The BAtlDir (page 416) cites only and echoes TIR Emerita (page 24) in describing the modern location of ad Herculem as "Novo Sancti Petri (Chiclana de la Frontera)"; however, neither BAtlas map 26 nor the TIR map place the symbol for ad Herculem anywhere nearly as far south as modern Novo Sancti Petri. The TIR map, in an inset at a scale of 1:250,000, places the station in a now-submerged area just offshore from the modern Playa de Sancti Petri, roughly due east of the Castillio de Sancti Petri (widely accepted location for the Hercules sanctuary). BAtlas 26 D5 at a scale of 1:500,000 opts for a location further north, roughly coincident with the place where a modern chapel stands on a peninsula named "Sancti Petri", site of piers, anchorages, and restaurants, as well as the dwindling remnants of older residences and structures.
description: An ancient station on the Roman road to Gades recorded in the Antonine Itinerary, ad Herculem must have been associated with the Herakleion on the southern end of the island of Cotinussa. Scholars differ on the precise location; their efforts are complicated by significant landscape change since antiquity.

description: The ancient name of this fortified grain-house is known only from a Latin inscription describing its restoration by a governor of Mauretaniae Caesariensis in the mid 290s CE under Diocletain and his tetrarchic colleagues. The inscription's findspot, near a spring in Algeria's Kefrida Pass depression, is close to remains of Roman fortifications noticed by French scholars in the 19th century on either side of the pass. They presumably guarded a road that ran south from Muslubium, as well as water sources (the "Aqua Frigida" itself?) supplying Muslubium via a recently discovered aqueduct (Ouaret Ladjouze). The modern toponymic component "K'frida" presumably reflects the ancient "Frigida".

title: Gabii
name_variants: Gabii@la | Gabies@fr | Castiglione@it | Gabii | Gabies | Castiglione | Gabii
details: Summary overview Gabii is an ancient city of Latium, located 18 km due east of Rome in central Italy. Located on the southeast side of the extinct volcanic crater of Castiglione, the site of Gabii is situated between the stream of the Fossa di San Giuliano to its east and the stream of the Osa to its west. To the south of the site is the line of the ancient Via Praenestina , a consular road of the Roman Republican period. The earlier road, known as the Via Gabina, connected Rome to Tibur. South of the line of the consular road lies another volcanic feature, the crater of Pantano, on whose northern extreme was a marshy area in antiquity. History of excavations The first 'excavation' known in the area of Gabii is the unscientific work of the art dealer and painter Gavin Hamilton (Hamilton 1901) in the late eighteenth century. Based on accounts in his own correspondence, Hamilton conducted excavations in the area of Gabii that recovered a large cache of high-quality Roman portrait sculpture and inscriptions. Hamilton believed he had excavated the forum of the city, as is reflected in a reconstructed plan published by E.Q. Visconti, but the matter is still debated (Visconti 1835). Many of Hamilton's 'finds' passed into the possession of the Borghese family at Rome and a number of pieces were relocated to the Louvre in Paris. For scientific excavation, we must fast forward to the twentieth century when excavations led by the Spanish Academy at Rome carried out extensive work on the sanctuary of Iuno Gabina located on the rim of the volcanic crater of Castiglione (Almagro Basch and Gorbea 1982). In the 1970s the site saw work on its 'eastern sanctuary' as well as field survey across the former urban area (Guaitoli 1981). A new field survey employing geophysics was carried out by the Gabii Project (University of Michigan) in 2007 and 2008, revealing the remains of an extensive system of quasi-orthogonal city streets beneath the surface (Becker, Mogetta, and Terrenato 2009). This survey served as the groundwork for an extensive series of excavations begun by Nicola Terrenato in 2009 and continuing. The excavations have revealed an almost one-hectare portion of the ancient city center. Other ongoing work at the site includes work of the local office of the Soprintendenza Speciale per i Beni Archeologici di Roma focused on the areas known as the 'area urbana' and 'Hamilton's Forum', work by a German team interested in the city walls (Helas 2010), and work by Stefano Musco and Marco Fabbri on an archaic elite compound on the rim of the volcanic crater. The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Castiglione
description: An ancient Latin city located on the line of the Republican Via Praenestina connecting Rome to Praeneste. Gabii is allied to Rome from an early date and flourished during the archaic period, declining by the time of Augustus.

title: Norba
name_variants: Norba@la | Νῶρβα@grc | Rovine di Norba@it | Norma@it | Norba | Rovine di Norba | Norma | Norba
details: Norba is an ancient settlement of Latium Adiectum located close to the modern town of Norma, Italy, in the Monti Lepini , also known as the Volscian Mountains. The ancient site occupies an impressive natural promontory that rises to over 1,500 feet above sea level and affords great visibility. Already a member of the Latin Leagues from 499 B.C., the site became a Latin colonia in 492 B.C., according to the historian Livy. The end of the ancient site came in 82 B.C. during the Sullan crisis when the city was laid waste by means of fire after having taken sides against Sulla. It would seem that the ruined city was not subsequently re-occupied in antiquity. The archaeological excavation of the site began in the early twentieth century with the work of L. Savignoni and R. Mengarelli (1901) (see reports in Notizie degli Scavi 1901 and 1904). Important aerial documentation of the site was carried out by Giulio Schmiedt for the Atlante aereofotografico delle sedi umane in Italia . In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, the site has been further excavated, with extensive work on areas adjacent to the forum and private domus in the vicinity of the minor acropolis. These excavations have been directed by Stefania Quilici-Gigli of the University of Naples. The site is an important urban center for the study of colonial sites in the Republican period, particularly the middle republic. Among the most notable archaeological remains visible at the site are those of the polygonal masonry fortification walls that enclose an area of more than 38 hectares.
description: Norba, located in the Monti Lepini, was a member of the Latin League (ca. 499 B.C.) and became a Latin colony ca. 492 B.C. The city was destroyed in the early first century B.C.

details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Sibari/Copia. Froelich Rainey (1969) offers a succinct summary of the settlement phases. Following the destruction of Sybaris ca. 510 BCE, there was a brief re-establishment of the city, but that, too, was razed. Athenians were encouraged to establish Thurii "near" the site of Sybaris in the fifth century BCE, a site famously planned by Hippodamos of Miletus. Lucanians then sacked Thurii ca. 390 BCE. The Roman Republic established a garrison at the site in 282 BCE. The ancient settlement lived until it was abandoned in the ninth century.

This topic is of particular interest to ancient authors, at least 70 of whom mention it.

title: Doliche | Dolica
name_variants: Doliche@la | Δολίχη@grc | Dolica@la | Doliche | Dolica
description: An ancient settlement of the Thessalian Perraibia. Precise localization of Doliche has a complex scholarly history. It was long assumed to be located in the vicinity of modern Dolichi/Duklista in Greece's Larisa regional unit (thus RE and BAtlas). Following the discovery of an extensive settlement site at Sarantaporo (8.5 kilometers west of modern Dolichi) in the 1990s, the excavators argued that it should be identified with ancient Doliche and this view has been widely repeated (e.g., New Pauly). More recently, the site of Kastri Livadiou (only about 4 km west southwest of modern Dolichi; 8.5 km southwest of modern Livadi) has been excavated. Here, a Late Antique walled settlement with three basilicas have been identified, together with inscriptions (found in conditions of reuse) attesting to an earlier temple of Herakles and, crucially, mentioning Doliche as a polis. The site at Sarantaporo may represent the original, Classical-to-Roman location of the polis, and the site at Kastri a later, fortified successor.

Without comment, Pliny places "fons Hyperia" immediately before "oppida Pherae" in a list of places in Thessaly (E. Kirsten in RE accepts this as a reference to the spring at Pherai, but BAtlDir lists it as an "unlocated spring in Thessaly"). Archaeological work confirms a perennial spring at Velestino was a locus of settlement activity from the Neolithic period onwards, and a structure monumentalizing the spring was built and modified during the Classical and Hellenistic periods.

title: Cortin[.]
name_variants: Γόρτυνα@grc | Cortin[.]@la | Gortyna | Gortyn | Ellotis | Kremnia | Larissa | Cortin[.] | Cortin[.]
details: Gortyna was inhabited continuously from the 8th century BC to the 9th century AD, and it is perhaps most famous for its law code dating from the 5th century BC. At the beginning of the 3rd century AD, the urban settlement underwent a major restructuring, with the building of an aqueduct 15 km long. The water supply system was renewed in the 6th century when the city was the seat of the Bishopric of Crete. The city was allegedly abandoned in the 9th century at the time of the Arab conquest of Crete, but it was already in decline following the misfortunes of the Byzantine sea supremacy and a series of major earthquakes. The site of ancient Gortyna is currently excavated by a joint team from the Universities of Bologna, Rome “La Sapienza“, Macerata, Palermo, Siena, Padova, Milano, coordinated by the Italian Archaeological School at Athens.
description: The Roman capital of Creta et Cyrenaica province, then Creta, and later seat of the Archbishop of Crete, Gortyna was a thriving community from the Geometric period to the Middle Byzantine period. The first traces of urban settlement date from the Archaic period. The ancient Greek law code known as the "Gortyn Code" was discovered there in 1884.

description: An ancient settlement of Phrygia, near the origin of the Mekestos river. Heavily spoliated, especially since the mid-19th century, and now cultivated, a Byzantine fortress on the hill immediately east of modern Boğazköy in Turkey's Kütahya province is uniformly identified with this ancient Ankyra. Many modern commentators have adopted the name "Ancyra Sidera" on the basis of an entry for a bishop in Latin and Syriac versions of the attendees the Council of Chalcedon (missing from the Greek witnesses), but Price 2010 asserts it may be a corruption of a lost original entry for a bishop of "Ancyra and Synaos".

title: Tricomia
name_variants: Τρικομία@grc | Tricomia@la | Trikomia | Tricomia | Tricomia
details: Ptolemy places this Trikomia in Φρυγία Μεγἀλης (Greater Phrygia), listing it between Μιδάϊον (Midaion) and Ἄγκυρα Φρυγίας (Phrygian Ankyra, i.e. modern Ankara) . The Peutinger Map places it on a route network between "Mideo" and "Pesinvnte" (i.e., Midaion and Pessinous ). " Dorileo " is one route segment leftward of "Mideo" on the Peutinger Map; therefore, the BAtlas Directory localizes Trikomia 3 "between Dorylaion and Pessinous". NB: A Wikipedia entry entitled "Tricomia (Phrygia)" conflates this Trikomia with another ( Pleiades 609560 ) that may have been located at modern İlkburun in Turkey. Such a view is implicitly rejected by RE and, following it, BAtlas and Pleiades .

title: Larissa
name_variants: Larissa@la | Larissa
details: Writing in the Barrington Atlas Directory for Map 64, T.B. Mitford cites T. Sinclair 1989 and suggests the following location for this Larissa: "vicinity of (H)Erp(h)a or on Karasekdüzü, 12 miles WSW Kangal?" (p. 993 s.v. "Larissa"). Sinclair 2020 (p. 179) demurs, tentatively placing Larissa at the point where the route of a Roman highway crosses the Zamantı river, but conceding that the distance figure as transmitted by the Peutinger map would have to be discarded as erroneous if his suggestion were accepted. It is worth noting in this context that the next Peutinger Map route segment beyond Larissa purports to go to "Incilissa" (see Pleiades Cilissa/Ingilissis ), which Mitford rejects as a place name entirely, considering it a corruption of "Cilicia" (BAtlDir p. 993 s.v. "Cilissa/Ingilissis"). The river crossing Sinclair prefers is where Mitford tentatively placed Euagina/Sebagina in BAtlas 64 C2 . Sinclair 2020 (p. 192 note 107) calls out what he sees as a discrepancy between the map position chosen by Mitford and the proper coordinates of the modern toponyms Mitford cites in the directory (p. 987 s.v. "Euagina/Sebagena?").
description: An ancient place in Cappadocia, lying on a Peutinger map route between "Arasaxa" and "Incilissa" (the latter possibly a false toponym resulting from scribal error). Modern attempts to identify a precise location are inconclusive.

details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Alep SYR Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 under criteria iii and iv of UNESCO's World Heritage List Operational Guidelines . Specific archaeological and cultural components highlighted in the World Heritage List entry include: Remains of Hittite, Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine and Ayyubid structures and elements are incorporated in the massive surviving Citadel . The diverse mixture of buildings including the Great Mosque founded under the Umayyads and rebuilt in the 12th century; the 12th century Madrasa Halawiye , which incorporates remains of Aleppo's Christian cathedral, together with other mosques and madrasas, suqs and khans represents an exceptional reflection of the social, cultural and economic aspects of what was once one of the richest cities of all humanity. Aleppo is an outstanding example of an Ayyubid 12th century city with its military fortifications constructed as its focal point following the success of Salah El-Din against the Crusaders. The encircling ditch and defensive wall above a massive, sloping, stone-faced glacis, and the great gateway with its machicolations comprise a major ensemble of military architecture at the height of Arab dominance. Works of the 13th-14th centuries including the great towers and the stone entry bridge reinforce the architectural quality of this ensemble. Surrounding the citadel within the city are numerous mosques from the same period including the Madrasah al Firdows , constructed by Daifa Khatoun in 1235.
description: The ancient city of Aleppo, located in modern Syria, where extensive elements of Hittite, Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Ayyubid, and Umayyad architecture are incorporated into the urban fabric of the modern city. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

name_variants: Carthaginiensis@la | Carthaginiensis

details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Viennensis
description: The Roman province of Aquitania Prima was established during the reforms of Diocletian in the late third century and assigned to the diocese of Viennensis. Avaricum Biturigum was its administrative capital.

title: Benetia Histria | Venetia et Histria
name_variants: Benetia Histria@la | Venetia et Histria@la | Benetia Histria | Venetia et Histria
details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Italia
description: According to the Verona List (ca. A.D. 303–324), Venetia et Histria was a province of the later Roman Empire located in northeastern Italy. It succeeded the tenth region (regio X) of the Augustan administrative re-organization. Diocletian reorganized the region to become "VIII provincia Venetia et Histria" in the third century CE. The capital was located at Aquileia. The province stretched from the Arsia River in the east to the Abdua in Lombardy.

title: Syria Coele
name_variants: Syria Coele@la | Syria Coele
details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Oriens
description: An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 101 P4 Syria Coele

details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Anatolike

title: Horti Domitiae Calvillae
name_variants: Horti Domitiae Calvillae@la | Horti Domitiae Calvillae
description: Gardens on the Caelian Hill that belonged to Domitia Calvilla, the mother of the emperor Marcus Aurelius. The future emperor was born and raised here.

title: porticus Eumenicae
name_variants: porticus Eumenicae@la | Stoa of Eumenes@en | porticus Eumenicae | Stoa of Eumenes | porticus Eumenicae
description: Eumenes II, king of Pergamon, built this eponymous stoa on the South slope of the Athenian Acropolis ca. 160 BCE. Its position lies between the Theater of Dionysus and the later Odeon of Herodes Atticus.

title: ad Malum Punicum
name_variants: ad Malum Punicum@la | ad Malum Punicum
description: Ad Malum Punicum describes a street on the Alta Semita in ancient Rome, likely corresponding to the modern Via delle Quattro Fontane. Vespasian owned a domus in this street and it was here that the future emperor Domitian was born.

title: Galaxia
name_variants: Galaxia@la | Galaxia
description: A place recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana that is to be located between Equizeto? and Auzia. Talbert notes that Galaxia is attested as a name on the manuscript, but has no symbol.

title: Avatha
name_variants: Avatha@la | Avatha
description: Avatha (al-Bakhra') is the site of a Late Roman and early Islamic fort that is located south of Palmyra. The fort was originally a Tetrarchic establishment that housed an auxiliary cavalry unit. The fort was modified and expanded during the Umayyad period.

title: Felignates
name_variants: Felignates@la | Felignates
description: An ancient people of Umbria whose territory is now unlocated.

title: Vicus Columnae Ligneae
name_variants: Vicus Columnae Ligneae@la | Vicus Columnae Ligneae
description: A street located in Regio XIII of ancient Rome that is mentioned on the so-called Capitoline Base (CIL 6, 975).

description: An ancient road that originated at Rome and continued to Castrum Truentinum (Porto d'Ascoli).

title: Basilica Sanctae Crucis in Hierusalem

description: A minor Catholic basilica in Rome, Santa Croce in Gerusalemme is also a titular church in rione Esquilino and one of the Seven Pilgrim Churches. The church was consecrated ca. 325 to house relics of the Passion of Jesus Christ brought to Rome from the Holy Land by Empress St. Helena.

title: ad Capita bubula
name_variants: ad Capita bubula@la | ad Capita bubula
description: The toponym "ad Capita bubula" is attested in Suetonius and refers to a place located at the northeast corner of the Palatine Hill in Rome near the Curiae Veteres. Here, there was a domus of one Caius Octavius, a Roman politician who was the biological father of Octavian. It is possible that Octavian was born in this domus, and the sources suggest that the location was later commemorated with the construction of a shrine (sacrarium) and, eventually, a temple.

title: Euganeae gentes
name_variants: Euganeae gentes@la | Euganeae gentes
description: Euganeae gentes describes an ancient confederation of pre-Roman peoples dwelling in northeast Italy, between the Adriatic Sea and the Alps. The exact nature of this group is difficult to define. Drawing upon Cato the Elder, Pliny the Elder asserts that the Euganeae gentes were divided into three groups: the Stoeni, the Triumpilini, and the Camuni.

title: Dabanegoris rĕgio
name_variants: Dabanegoris rĕgio@la | Dabanegoris regio | Dabanegoris rĕgio
description: A region of Arabia mentioned by Pliny the Elder.

title: Ostudizo
name_variants: Ostudizo@la | Ostudizo
details: Possibly to be identified with Hostino or Hostizo in Tabula Peutingeriana. Löhberg locates it near the city of Havsa in Turkey.
description: City in Thrace located on the road between Hadrianopolis and Byzantium, attested in the Antonine Itinerary.

title: Guthalus
name_variants: Guthalus@la | Guthalus
description: Pliny includes the Guthalus in a list of rivers of Germania that flow into the North Sea.

title: Porta Capena
name_variants: Porta Capena@la | Porta Capena
description: The Porta Capena was a gate in Rome's Republican city walls ("Servian Wall") located on the south-west slope of the Caelian Hill.

title: Porta Esquilina
name_variants: Porta Esquilina@la | Arch of Gallienus@en | Porta Esquilina | Arch of Gallienus | Porta Esquilina
description: The Arch of Gallienus marked the Porta Esquilina, a gate in the Servian Wall of Rome. The via Labicana and via Tiburtina issue from Rome at this point. The arch was erected in A.D. 262.

title: silva Ciminia
name_variants: silva Ciminia@la | silva Ciminia
description: A forest in ancient Etruria that was a feared and trackless wilderness in the middle Republican period.

title: Silua Maesia
name_variants: Silua Maesia@la | Silva Maesia | Silua Maesia
details: Pliny comments on the forest in the context of his discussion of the habits of dormice.
description: An ancient forest of Etruria that originally was situated in the territory of Veii. Ancus Marcus conquered the area which most likely was located on the right bank of the Tiber.

title: fons Bandusiae
name_variants: fons Bandusiae@la | fons Bandusiae
description: The Latin poet Horace addresses one of his odes to the Fons Bandusiae (Spring of Bandusium). Its precise location remains a matter of discussion.

title: Gelvina
name_variants: Gelvina@la | Gelvina
description: A place located in north-eastern Armenia, some 20 Roman miles from Artaxata, on the main road to Harmastica.

title: porta Naevia
name_variants: porta Naevia@la | porta Naevia
description: The now-lost Porta Naevia was a minor gate in the Republican-period wall of the city of Rome. It was located on the Little Aventine and its position may correspond to the modern Largo Enzo Fioritto.

title: Lupanar
name_variants: Lupanar@la | Lupanare Grande@it | Lupanar | Lupanare Grande | Lupanar
description: The Lupanar (or Lupanare Grande) (VII, 12, 18–20) is located east of the forum at the intersection of Vico del Lupanare and Vico del Balcone Pensile. It is the largest of Pompeii's brothels.

title: Tuledo
name_variants: Monte Leco@it | Tuledo@la | Monte Lecco@it | Monte Leco | Tuledo | Monte Lecco | Tuledo
details: CIL V, 7749 mentions this place name: in montem Apeninum quei vocatur Boplo.
description: A mountain in the Ligurian Apennines cited in the Sententia Minuciorum; the modern Monte Leco.

title: Via *Quinctia
name_variants: Via *Quinctia@la | Via Quinctia@it | Via *Quinctia | Via Quinctia | Via *Quinctia

title: Corycius specus

description: A large karstic grotto and cave, known today as Cennet ve Cehennem, which is located about 7km from Corycus in Cilicia. It was described by Mela, Apollodorus, and Strabo and was associated with the Titan Python in Greek mythology. It is not to be confused with the well-known Corycian Cave on mount Parnassos in Greece.

title: Domus Clementis
name_variants: Domus Clementis@la | Domus Clementis
description: The remains of a private domus that date to the second and third centuries CE and include a Mithraeum. This complex eventually became incorporated into the fourth-century basilica on the site of the later basilica of San Clemente al Laterano.

title: Hercules Sullanus
name_variants: Hercules Sullanus@la | Hercules Sullanus
description: Either a statue or shrine of Hercules located in Regio V somewhere east of the Piazza Vittorio Emanuele, perhaps close to the nymphaeum known as the Temple of Minerva Medica. Whether the site was, in fact, connected to Lucius Cornelius Sulla is debated.

title: Portus Boeotorum
name_variants: Portus Boeotorum@la | Portus Boeotorum
description: Portus Boeotorum is a place included on the Peutinger map. It would have been located near Kallatis in the Roman province of Moesia Inferior.

title: Fundus Braetianus
name_variants: Fundus Braetianus@la | Fundus Braetianus
description: Fundus Braetianus, a toponym included on the Trajanic alimentary table from Veleia.

title: Meta Romuli
name_variants: Meta Romuli@la | Piramide vaticana@it | Piramide di Borgo@it | Meta Romuli | Piramide vaticana | Piramide di Borgo | Meta Romuli
description: The so-called "Meta Romuli" was a pyramidal tomb located in the Ager Vaticanus in Rome. It likely dates to the first century BCE or the first century CE. Its extant superstructure was demolished in 1499. Remains of foundations and pavements that have been associated with the tomb were encountered in 1948-1949 during construction work in the first block of the north side of the present-day Via della Conciliazione.

title: Trebiates
name_variants: Trebiates@la | Trebiates
description: An ancient tribe of Umbria that Pliny places in the sixth Augustan region.

title: Porta Flaminia
name_variants: Porta del Popolo@it | Porta Flaminia@la | Porta del Popolo | Porta Flaminia | Porta Flaminia
description: A gate in the Aurelian Wall from which the Via Flaminia issued, the Porta Flaminia became known as the Porta del Popolo after the fifteenth century. Sixtus IV is credited with building the gateway that stands today.

title: Porta Fontinalis
name_variants: Porta Fontinalis@la | Porta Fontinalis
description: No longer extant, the Porta Fontinalis is only known via textual and epigraphic references. Presumed to be a gate of the Servian Wall, the Porta Fontinalis lay in the Campus Martius, west of the via Lata. It may have been the original point of issuance for the Republican roads known as the Via Flaminia and the Via Salaria.

title: Flacciana
name_variants: Flacciana@la | Flacciana
description: A place in Africa Proconsularis, according to the Peutinger map.

title: Velina
name_variants: Velina@la | Velina
details: The tribus Velina was organised when Curius Dentatus was censor. Its name derives from the Lacus Velinus, but its location was most likely on the Adriatic coast, presumably in the territory of the Praetuttii .
description: The tribus Velina was one of the later rural tribes which was established in Rome in 241 B.C.

title: Pons Fabricius
name_variants: Ponte dei Quattro Capi@it | Pons Fabricius@la | Ponte dei Quattro Capi | Pons Fabricius | Pons Fabricius
description: The Pons Fabricius (sometimes referred to as the Ponte dei Quattro Capi) is a first-century BC bridge in Rome that spans part of the Tiber River from the area of the Circus Flaminius to the Tiber Island.

title: Circus Varianus
name_variants: Circus Varianus@la | Circus Varianus
description: A circus that was part of the Sessorium palace next to the Amphitheatrum Castrense. The obelisk currently situated on the Pincian Hill was discovered on the site in the sixteenth century. It had been moved to the spina of the circus during the reign of Elagabalus.

title: forum olitorium | Forum holitorium
name_variants: forum olitorium@la | Forum holitorium@la | Foro Olitorio@it | forum olitorium | Forum holitorium | Foro Olitorio | forum olitorium | Forum holitorium
description: The Forum Holitorium was the vegetable market of ancient Rome, situated outside the Porta Carmentalis in the southern Campus Martius. This area was bounded by the Forum Boarium and the Circus Flaminius.

title: Labyrinthus
name_variants: λαβύρινθον@grc | Labyrinthus@la | Labyrinthos | Labyrinthus | Labyrinthus
description: Legendary, mythological labyrinth in the palace of Knossos built by mythic figure Daedalus to house the monster Minotaur.

title: salt(us) Firronani
name_variants: salt(us) Firronani@la | Firronanus Saltus | salt(us) Firronani
details: Transpadana (Regio XI)
description: The pontifex Lucius Coelius Baro is recorded as the curator of the Firronanus Saltus located in regio XI.

title: via Labicana | Via lauicana
name_variants: via Labicana@la | Via lauicana@la | via Labicana | uia Labicana | Labicana (via) | Labicana (uia) | Via Lavicana | via Labicana | Via lauicana
description: An ancient Roman road connecting Rome and Labicum.

title: Castrum Rauracense
name_variants: Castrum Rauracense@la | Kaiseraugst@de | Castrum Rauracense | Kaiseraugst | Castrum Rauracense
description: A Late Roman fortress located on the southern bank of the Rhine adjacent to Augusta Raurica.

title: Pallantium
name_variants: Pallantium@la | Pallantium
description: Legend held that Pallantium, founded by Evander of Pallene, was located near the Tiber and was an urban precursor of the city of Rome. The site is most famously discussed in the Aeneid of Virgil.

title: Templum Claudii | Templum divi Claudii
name_variants: Templum Claudii@la | Templum divi Claudii@la | Temple of Claudius@en | Templum Claudii | Templum divi Claudii | Temple of Claudius | Claudius (Temple of) | Templum Claudii | Templum divi Claudii
description: A large classical-style Roman temple built shortly after the conquest of Britannia in A.D. 43 by the emperor Claudius. Its remains lie beneath Colchester Castle.

title: vicus vitrarius
name_variants: vicus vitrarius@la | vicus vitrarius
description: A street in Regio I known only from the Regionary Catalogues.

title: Simitta
name_variants: Simitta@la | Simitta
description: A place included on the Peutinger map, lying along the route from Batnae/Markopolis to another unlocated place marked as "Vicus".

title: pars oppius
name_variants: pars oppius@la | pars oppius
description: The Oppian Hill is the southern spur of Rome's Esquiline Hill.

title: Stadium
name_variants: Stadium@la | Stadium of Domitian@en | Piazza Navona@it | Stadium | Stadium of Domitian | Piazza Navona | Stadium
description: Domitian built the Stadium Domitiani in the Campus Martius at Rome.

title: Hermupolis
name_variants: Hermupolis@la | Hermupolis
description: A place in Carmania, known only from literary sources.

title: Via Latina
name_variants: Via Latina@la | Λατινὴ ὁδός, ἡ@grc | Via Latina | Latine hodos | Via Latina
details: The road likely predates the construction of the Via Appia.
description: A Roman road running southeast from Rome toward Campania.

title: Porticus Divorum
name_variants: Porticus Divorum@la | Porticus Divorum
description: A porticus constructed by Domitian in A.D. 80 on the eastern Campus Martius on the site of the Villa Publica, whose northern entry—a triumphal arch—was flanked by two small temples in honor of Titus and Vespasian.

title: VII.4.1
name_variants: Tempio della Fortuna@it | Temple of Victory@en | Aedes of Fortuna Augusta@en | Temple of Serapis@en | VII.4.1@la | Tempio della Fortuna | Temple of Victory | Aedes of Fortuna Augusta | Temple of Serapis | VII.4.1 | VII.4.1

title: Schola Quaestorum et Caplatorum
name_variants: Schola Quaestorum et Caplatorum@la | Schola Quaestorum et Caplatorum
description: The Schola Quaestorum et Caplatorum is a place in ancient Rome that is mentioned only in the Regionary Catalogue for Regio III. It was likely located between the lacus Pastorum and the Baths of Titus. While the name and place remain obscure, related epigraphic evidence attests to collegia of caplatores, men who pressed olive oil.

title: Cvrrapho
name_variants: Cvrrapho@la | Currapho | Cvrrapho
description: Currapho, a place in Mesopotamia included on the Peutinger map.

title: BRVSDORCIANI
name_variants: BRVSDORCIANI@la | Brusdorciani | BRVSDORCIANI
description: An ancient people whose territory was located in Thrace on the Hebros near Adrianople.

title: Darsa
name_variants: Darsa@la | Darsa
description: An ancient city in Pisidia.

title: Murus Servii Tullii
name_variants: Murus Servii Tullii@la | Mura serviane@it | Servian Wall@en | Murus Servii Tullii | Mura serviane | Servian Wall | Murus Servii Tullii
description: The Republican city wall of Rome.

title: Vaticanus Ager
name_variants: Vaticanus Ager@la | Vaticanus Ager
description: A district on the right bank of the river Tiber, between the lower course of the river and the territory of Veii.

title: Iuppiter Arborator
name_variants: Iuppiter Arborator@la | Iuppiter Arborator
description: A place included in Regio XI of the Regionary Catalogues, this may have been a shrine on the spina of the Circus Maximus.

title: Tabernae veteres
name_variants: Tabernae veteres@la | Tabernae veteres
description: The so-called Tabernae Veteres were shops built in the valley of the Forum Romanum. The textual tradition assigns responsibility for this project to Lucius Tarquinius Priscus. The state owned the shops and leased them to tenants.

title: Empulum
name_variants: Empulum@la | Empulum
details: Empulum was an outlying town connected to Tibur. The Romans captured it ca. 355 B.C. It may have been a fortified site. Both Gell and Nibby discussed the site, connecting it with the locality of Ampiglione, along the road to Ciciliano in Lazio, some 35 km east of Rome. The nineteenth-century commentators remark that this fortified site has evidence of "polygonal work", i.e., polygonal masonry, executed in tuff, something that even Smith (1854) remarks upon as being unusual since polygonal masonry is typically executed in calcareous stone, notably limestone. Giovenale (1900, fig. 6) describes these walls as "polyhedric megalithic" and notes that they employ a lithoid tuff as would be expected for this part of Latium.

description: A Roman vicus, attested by name in inscriptions discovered in the 19th century. Based on the reported findspots of the inscriptions, the vicus seems to have been located in the vicinity of modern Spechbach, located southeast of Heidelberg, Germany.

title: Cercina
name_variants: Cercina@la | Cercina
description: A now-unlocated place near Florentia in Etruria (Regio VII) known from epigraphic sources. Caius Caesar, the father of Iulius Caesar, helmed a veterans' colony there.

title: flumen Quosenum
name_variants: flumen Quosenum@la | flumen Quosenum
description: Pliny the Elder mentions a river named Quosenum in the context of his discussion of the voyage of the historian Polybius beyond the Atlas Mountains that was said to have been facilitated by Scipio Aemilianus.

title: Forum Traiani | Forum Ulpium
name_variants: Forum Traiani@la | Forum Ulpium@la | Forum of Trajan@en | Forum Traiani | Forum Ulpium | Forum of Trajan | Forum Traiani | Forum Ulpium
description: Imperial forum constructed at Rome under Trajan between 105-112 CE.

title: Domus Augusti
name_variants: House of Augustus@en | Domus Augusti@la | Casa di Augusto@it | House of Augustus | Domus Augusti | Casa di Augusto | Domus Augusti
description: An elite domus located at the southwest corner of the Palatine Hill that is identified as the house lived in by the Roman emperor Augustus.

title: Privata domus Traiani
name_variants: Privata domus Traiani@la | Privata domus Traiani
description: The so-called "Privata domus Traiani" was an opulent townhouse on the Aventine Hill in Rome. Its foundations were eventually coopted in the third century CE for the construction of the Baths of Decius. Evidence from brickstamps dates the building to the Trajanic to early Antonine period, leading some scholars to suggest that Marcus Ulpius Traianus occupied this domus before his adoption by Nerva.

title: Boecolen Montes
name_variants: Boecolen Montes@la | Βαικολικὸν ὄρος@grc | Boecolen Montes | Baikolikòn óros | Boecolen Montes
description: A mountain range located in southern Cyrenaica.

title: Palatini Apollinis templum | templum Apollinis in Palatio
title_ipa: palatini apollinis templum | templum apollinis in palatio
name_variants: Palatini Apollinis templum@la | templum Apollinis in Palatio@la | Palatini Apollinis templum | templum Apollinis in Palatio
description: The temple sacred to the god Apollo on the Palatine Hill in Rome.

title: Romilia
name_variants: Romilia@la | Romilia
details: The location of the tribus Romilia on the right bank of the Tiber river is uncertain. Its name derives from the Roman gens Romilia .
description: An older rural tribe of ancient Rome that was located at the edge of Etruscan territory, across the river Tiber.

title: Templum Veneris et Romae | templum urbis Romae
title_ipa: templum veneris et rome | templum urbis rome
name_variants: Templum Veneris et Romae@la | templum urbis Romae@la | Temple of Venus and Rome@en | Tempio di Venere e Roma@it | Tempel der Venus und Roma@de | Templum Veneris et Romae | templum urbis Romae | Temple of Venus and Rome | Tempio di Venere e Roma | Tempel der Venus und Roma | Templum Veneris et Romae | templum urbis Romae
description: A double temple sacred to Venus Felix and Roma Aeterna built by Hadrian on the slope of the Velian hill to the north of the Sacra Via beginning in 121 CE.

title: Telmi
name_variants: Telmi@la | Telmi
description: Telmi is a place included on the Peutinger map along the route from Taskry (Tasdri) to Tenis he kai Hakoreos (Acori).

title: Clivus Scauri
name_variants: Clivus Scauri@la | Clivus Scauri
description: A street that ascended from the depression between the Palatine and the Caelian hills.

title: porta Collina
name_variants: porta Collina@la | Porta Collina | porta Collina
description: The Porta Collina was a gate in Rome's Servian Wall located on the Quirinal Hill. At the Porta Collina the Via Salaria and the Via Nomentana divided. Some remains of the gate were identified in 1872 on the Via Venti Settembre beneath the Italian Ministry of Finance.

title: Via Aurelia Aeclanensis?
name_variants: Via Aurelia Aeclanensis?@la | Via Aurelia Aeclanensis?
description: A road in Apulia leading from Aeclanum toward Vibinum. The Via Aurelia Aeclanensis? intersects the Via Herculia.

title: Via Collatina
name_variants: Via Collatina@la | Via Collatina
description: A Roman road connecting Rome with Collatia.

title: uia Tiburtina, via Tiburtina | Via Tybvrtina
title_ipa: uia tiburtina via tiburtina | via tibvrtina
name_variants: uia Tiburtina, via Tiburtina@la | Via Tybvrtina@la | via Tiburtina | Via Tyburtina | uia Tiburtina, via Tiburtina | Via Tybvrtina
description: An ancient road heading east-northeast from Rome to Tibur.

title: adfl. Ganges
name_variants: adfl. Ganges@la | Ad flumen Ganges | adfl. Ganges
description: Ad flumen Ganges is a place marked on the Peutinger Map.

title: Presididiolele | Presidio diolele
name_variants: Presididiolele@la | Presidio diolele@la | Presididiolele | Presidio diolele
description: An ancient place in North Africa that is included on the Peutinger map.

title: Aedes divi Iulii
name_variants: Aedes divi Iulii@la | Aedes divi Iulii
description: The temple on the Sacra Via dedicated to the deified Iulius Caesar, authorized in 42 B.C. and built by Augustus, with its dedication occurring on 18th August, 29 B.C.

title: Alburnus Maior
name_variants: Alburnus Maior@la | Roșia Montană@ro | Alburnus Maior | Roșia Montană | Rosia Montana | Alburnus Maior
details: Barrington Atlas Directory: Roşia Montană ROM
description: A settlement and gold mining complex at modern Roşia Montană in Romania. The Roșia Montană Mining Landscape was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021.

title: Redones
name_variants: Redones@la | Redones
description: A Celtic tribe living in the area of modern Brittany counted among the civitates maritimae or Aremorica.

title: Abara
name_variants: Abara@la | Abara
description: A place included in the Peutinger map.

title: Amphitheatrum Flavium
name_variants: Amphitheatrum Flavium@la | Flavian amphitheater@en | Colosseum@en | Colosseo@it | Kolosseum@de | Anfiteatro Flavio@it | Amphitheatrum Flavium | Flavian amphitheater | Colosseum | Colosseo | Kolosseum | Anfiteatro Flavio | Amphitheatrum Flavium
description: The Flavian amphitheater at Rome (the so-called "Colosseum").

title: pons sublicius
name_variants: Pons Theodosii@la | pons sublicius@la | Pons Theodosii | pons Sublicius | pons sublicius
description: The Pons Sublicius is traditionally held to be the earliest Roman bridge across the river Tiber. The textual tradition assigns its construction to the king Ancus Marcius in 642 B.C. It crossed the Tiber River near the Forum Boarium just downstream from Tiber Island.

title: at Tres Silanos
name_variants: at Tres Silanos@la | Ad tres Silanos | at Tres Silanos
details: The inscription attesting to the toponym is housed in the Antiquario dell'Abbazia di S. Nilo in Grottaferrata (Roma).
description: Ad Tres Silanos is a toponym associated with the ancient city of Rome but attested in a Latin inscription found at Grottaferrata. The inscription refers to a group of three fountains known by the typological name 'silanus' located in Regio VII.

title: Iovis tifatinvs
name_variants: Iovis tifatinvs@la | Iovis tifatinus | Iovis tifatinvs
description: A sanctuary sacred to Jupiter located on the western slopes of Tifata Mons (Monte Tifata).

title: Ligar
name_variants: Ligar@la | Ligar
description: "Ligar" is provided as a name for a river in Mauretania Caesariensis by the Ravenna Cosmographer (ed. Schnetz). Gsell (AAA) views "Ligar" as a mistake or corruption for "Siga". Neither Schnetz (in his apparatus) nor BAtlDir address the issue. BAtlas/BAtlDir does not include "Ligar" at all.

title: Regio X Palatium
name_variants: Regio X Palatium@la | Regio X Palatium
description: Regio X (Palatium) is one of the Augustan regions of the city of Rome. The Regionary Catalogues indicate that this regio contained 20 shrines (aediculae), 89 townhouses (domūs), 48 warehouses (horrea), 44 bath houses, and 89 fountains. Its perimeter was recorded as 11,510 Roman feet (approx. 3.4 km).

title: Carbania
name_variants: Carbania@la | Carbania
description: An island in the Tyrrhenian Sea mentioned by Pomponius Mela that is now unlocated. C. Hülsen suggested that this could be the same as the unlocated island "Barpana" mentioned by Pliny the Elder in his Natural History.

title: [T]heatrum Marcelli
name_variants: Teatro di Marcello@it | [T]heatrum Marcelli@la | Theater of Marcellus@en | Teatro di Marcello | Theatrum Marcelli | Theater of Marcellus | [T]heatrum Marcelli
description: Theatrum Marcelli (Theater of Marcellus) is an ancient Roman theater in the Circus Flaminius. Augustus completed its construction and dedicated it in 12 BC.

title: Hic Alexander Responsvm accepit Vsq(ve) qvo Alexander
title_ipa: hik aleksander responsvm akkepit vsqve qvo aleksander
name_variants: Hic Alexander Responsvm accepit Vsq(ve) qvo Alexander@la | Hic Alexander Responsum accepit usque quo Alexander | Hic Alexander Responsvm accepit Vsq(ve) qvo Alexander
details: Richard Talbert translates the Latin as follows: "Here Alexander received the response [from Stoics and demons]: 'Only this far, Alexander'."
description: This Latin legend is marked on the manuscript of the Tabula Peutingeriana in the general vicinity of the city of Alexandria Eschate. Posed as a rhetorical question, this text may corroborate a story related in the Alexander Romance relating to Alexander's seeming insatiable appetite for territorial conquest.

title: Porta Trigemina
name_variants: Porta Trigemina@la | Porta Trigemina
description: Now lost, the Porta Trigemina was one of the main gates of the Servian Wall.

title: Castrum Perticae
name_variants: Castrum Perticae@la | Castrum Perticae
description: A fortified site of the later Byzantine period located at Finale Ligure.

title: fanum Quietis
name_variants: fanum Quietis@la | fanum Quietis
description: A shrine sacred to Quies on the Via Labicana. It is mentioned by Livy in the fourth book of his history as he discusses movements of Roman forces engaged with the Volscians.

title: arcus propter aedem Saturni
name_variants: arcus propter aedem Saturni@la | arcus propter aedem Saturni
description: A single-bay triumphal arch dedicated to Tiberius in 16 CE. This arch commemorated the recovery of Varus' standards lost in 9 CE. It stood on the Sacra Via at the northwest corner of the Basilica Iulia.

title: Otesini
name_variants: Otesini@la | Otesini
description: An ancient tribe of northern Italy, perhaps located in the vicinity of Bononia.

title: Uetus Claudia tribus
name_variants: Uetus Claudia tribus@la | vetus Claudia tribus | Uetus Claudia tribus
details: The tribus Claudia was organized ca. 504 B.C. by Attius Clausus (also know more commonly as Appius Claudius). The tribal territory lay north of the Anio river, between Fidenae and Ficulea. The tribus Claudia adjoined the tribus Clustumina.
description: The tribus Claudia was the twenty-first rural tribe.

title: portus Iulius
name_variants: portus Iulius@la | portus Iulius
description: The so-called "Portus Iulius" is an ancient Roman port complex on the Bay of Naples. Its remains are now submerged due to the bradyseism of the Phlegraean Fields. The archaeological remains were first rediscovered in 1956.

title: Mysomacedones
name_variants: Mysomacedones@la | Μυσομακέδονες@grc | Mysomacedones | Mysomakedones | Mysomacedones
description: A tribe located in the area of Ephesus, concentrated on the area around the river Mysius.

title: Area Carruces
name_variants: Area Carruces@la | Area Carruces
description: Mentioned only in the Regionary Catalogues, the Area Carruces was perhaps a square where travelers were accustomed to leaving their carriages.

title: uicus Longus
name_variants: uicus Longus@la | Vicus Longus | uicus Longus
description: The Vicus Longus was a street in ancient Rome that linked the Quirinal Hill to the Suburra.

title: flumen Apilas
name_variants: flumen Apilas@la | flumen Apilas
description: The Apilas was an ancient river of Macedonia. Its name and location today is uncertain.

title: Pons Agrippae
name_variants: Pons Agrippae@la | Pons Agrippae
description: A debated bridge upriver from the modern Ponte Sisto.

title: Niger lapis
name_variants: Niger lapis@la | Niger lapis
details: Filippo Coarelli interprets the archaic remains beneath the pavement of the Lapis Niger as being elements of the Volcanal, an archaic sanctuary of the god Vulcan.
description: A shrine in the Forum Romanum adjacent to the Republican comitium, recognizable by the distinctive black paving stones that covered it in the later republican period. The shrine has been associated, in tradition, with the tomb of Romulus and/or of Faustulus. Giacomo Boni excavated the site between 1899 and 1905.

title: Macellum Magnum
name_variants: Macellum Magnum@la | μάκελλον@grc | Macellum Magnum | makellon | Macellum Magnum
description: The emperor Nero built the great market hall on the Caelian Hill and dedicated it in the year 59. The market hall is known from numismatic imagery and some of its archaeological remains have been documented on the Caelian Hill.

title: Mecium
name_variants: Mecium@la | Mecium
description: Maecium or Mecium is a locality near Lanuvium where the Volsci encamped.

title: Caledoni
name_variants: Δουηκαληδονίοι@grc-Linb | Καληδόνιοι@grc | Caledoni@la | Douekaledonioi | Kaledonioi | Caledoni | Caledoni
description: A people located in what is now eastern Scotland (Caledonia) prior to and during the Roman period.

title: Pons Aelius | Ponte adriani
name_variants: Ponte Sant'Angelo@it | Pons Aelius@la | Ponte adriani@la | Ponte Sant'Angelo | Pons Aelius | Ponte adriani | Pons Aelius | Ponte adriani
details: The Pons Aelius is one of 9 Tiber River bridges included on map 43 of the Barrington Atlas. These bridges are not necessarily specified by name, given the scale of the map, but the compilers have used Richardson's 1992 listing as their guide.
description: The Pons Aelius or Aelian Bridge (now Ponte Sant'Angelo) was completed by Hadrian in AD 134 to span the Tiber opposite the new mausoleum of the emperor.

title: Mausoleum Hadriani
name_variants: Mausoleum Hadriani@la | Hadrian's mole@en | Mausoleum Hadriani | Hadrian's mole | Mausoleum Hadriani
description: Mausoleum Hadriani (now Castel Sant'Angelo) located on the right bank of the Tiber River was an imperial mausoleum built by Hadrian between 134 and 139 CE. It continued as a tomb for subsequent emperors through to Caracalla, who died in 217 CE. By 401 the tomb had become a fortress with Honorius incorporating it into the line of the Aurelianic walls. During Alaric's sacking of Rome in 410 the mausoleum was looted and the ash urns dispersed. Procopius describes the destruction of the tomb's bronze statuary in 537. By the fourteenth century, the mausoleum had become a papal fortress. At one point, a fortified corridor known as Passetto di Borgo connected the fortress to St. Peter's Basilica.

title: Balneum | Balneae | Balineae | Thermae minores
name_variants: Pubbliche terme@it | Bain public@fr | Bagni pubblici@it | Terme pompeiane@it | Bagni antichi@it | Piccola terma@it | Piccole terme@it | Terme minori@it | Terme della Fortuna@it | Forumsthermen@de | Terme del Foro@it | Balneum@la | Balneae@la | Balineae@la | Thermae@en | Thermae minores@la | VII.5.2@en | Pubbliche terme | Bain public | Bagni pubblici | Terme pompeiane | Bagni antichi | Piccola terma | Piccole terme | Terme minori | Terme della Fortuna | Forumsthermen | Terme del Foro | Balneum | Balneae | Balineae | Thermae | Thermae minores | VII.5.2 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 17 | 18 | 24 | Balneum | Balneae | Balineae | Thermae minores
description: A bath complex adjacent to Pompeii's forum that was built after 80 BC (Reg VII, Ins 5, 2, 5, 7, 24). The baths are publicly financed by the duovir Lucius Caesius and the aediles Caius Occius and Lucius Niraemius.

title: Vico Valeriani
name_variants: Vico Valeriani@la | Vico Valeriani
description: Vicus Valeriani is attested in the Tabula Peutingeriana as Vico Valeriani.

title: Vasconum saltus
name_variants: Vasconum saltus@la | Vasconum saltus
description: A forest, now unlocated, in the territory of the Varduli.

title: curiae veteres
name_variants: curiae veteres@la | Curiae Veteres | curiae veteres
description: The earliest sanctuary of the curiae at Rome, located at the northeastern corner of the Palatine Hill. Tacitus identifies the structure as one point of the Palatine pomerium.

title: Porticus Philippi
name_variants: Porticus Philippi@la | Porticus Philippi
description: A portico that surrounded the Temple of Hercules Musarum in the Campus Martius of ancient Rome. The construction of the portico was the result of the patronage of L. Marcius Philippus, the stepfather of Augustus.

title: mons Tarpeius | mons Capitolinus
name_variants: mons Tarpeius@la | Monte Capitolino@it | Capitoline Hill@en | mons Capitolinus@la | mons Tarpeius | Monte Capitolino | Capitoline Hill | mons Capitolinus | mons Tarpeius | mons Capitolinus
description: The smallest of Rome's hills and one of its most important, the Capitoline Hill served as the citadel (arx) of the city and as the site of its poliadic temple.

title: porta Querquetulana
name_variants: porta Querquetulana@la | porta Querquetulana
description: The Porta Querquetulana was a gateway of Rome's so-called Servian Walls. It derived its name from from a sacred grove of oaks that seems to have vanished by the first century BCE.

title: Caesareum
name_variants: Caesareum@la | Ginnasio dello stato@it | Ginnasio-Cesareo@it | Forum of Proculus@en | Caesareum | Ginnasio dello stato | Ginnasio-Cesareo | Forum of Proculus | Caesareum
description: A large architectural complex on the east side of the acropolis ridge in Cyrene that was probably built at the beginning of the first century AD and used as a gymnasium, but was later repurposed as forum in Flavian times, when the rooms north of the complex were levelled in order to build a large basilica. Various ruins can still be seen, including the podium of a temple in the central area, possibly dedicated to Dionysos. A fragmentary inscription referring to the "portico of Caesar", found over the inner side of the porch, made the place known as Caesareum.

title: Tonantis Iouis
name_variants: Tonantis Iouis@la | Tonantis Iouis
description: A small temple to Jupiter the Thunderer, most likely located in the Area Capitolina. Vowed by Augustus in 26 BCE and dedicated in 22 BCE.

title: porta Rauduscula
name_variants: porta Rauduscula@la | porta Rauduscula
description: The Porta Rauduscula was a gate of Rome's so-called Servian Wall. It is known only from textual sources. Varro's listing places it between the Porta Naevia and the Porta Lavernalis.

title: Uicae Potae
name_variants: Uicae Potae@la | ἱερόν Οὐίκας Πότας@grc | Vicae Potae aedes | hieron Ouikias Potas | Uicae Potae
description: A shrine built by Publius Valerius on the slope of the Velia facing the Forum Romanum.

title: domus Cilonis
name_variants: domus Cilonis@la | domus Cilonis
description: The house of Lucius Fabius Cilo, praefectus urbi in 203, consul in 193 and 204, and a close friend of the emperor Septimius Severus. The house was a gift of the Severans and appears on the Severan marble plan. Its site is now occupied by the basilica of Santa Balbina on the "little Aventine".

title: uia Appia; Via Appia
name_variants: uia Appia; Via Appia@la | ἡ Ἀππία ὁδός@grc | Via Appia Antica@it | Via Appia | Appia odos | Via Appia Antica | uia Appia; Via Appia
details: In July 2024, the Via Appia was inscribed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO. This cultural property, under the title of "Via Appia. Regina Viarum, " conceives of the remains of the 800-km-long Via Appia as a cultural landscape; this heritage "site" comprises remains stretching from Rome to Brindisi. In inscribing the site on the World Heritage list, UNESCO lists the area of the heritage site itself as 4,639.92 hectares with a buffer zone of 40,205.79 hectares. UNESCO enrolled the site as it meets the following criteria: (iii) to bear a unique or at least exceptional testimony to a cultural tradition or to a civilization which is living or which has disappeared; (iv) to be an outstanding example of a type of building, architectural or technological ensemble or landscape which illustrates (a) significant stage(s) in human history; (v) to be an outstanding example of a traditional human settlement, land-use, or sea-use which is representative of a culture (or cultures), or human interaction with the environment, especially when it has become vulnerable under the impact of irreversible change;
description: An early Roman road (via publica) originating at Rome and terminating at Brundisium, the Via Appia was begun in the fourth century B.C. by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus. The Latin author Statius described the Via Appia as "queen of the long roads".

title: *Via Curia
name_variants: *Via Curia@la | *Via Curia | Via Curia | *Via Curia
description: A Roman road connecting Reate (Rieti) with Interamna Nahars (Terni).

title: Mucia prata
name_variants: Mucia prata@la | Μούκιοι λειμῶνες@grc | Mucia prata | Moukioi leimones | Mucia prata
description: The so-called Prata Mucia was a meadow granted to the Roman Republican hero Mucius Scaevola in recognition of his heroism in the face of the invasion of Lars Porsena of Clusium. While it was located on the right bank of the River Tiber, a precise location cannot be ascertained.

title: Pagus Ianiculensis
name_variants: Pagus Ianiculensis@la | Pagus Ianiculensis
description: Pagus Ianiculens is a name for a district of the Transtiberim during the Republican period. The name is attested in two inscriptions of ca. 100 B.C., one of which was found in an opus signinum pavement near the church of Santa Maria dell'Orto.

title: Basilica Neptuni
name_variants: Basilica Neptuni@la | στόα Ποσειδῶνος@grc | Basilica Neptuni | stoa Poseidonos | Basilica Neptuni
description: A building in the Campus Martius that originally dates to ca. 25 BCE.

title: Gelotiana
name_variants: Gelotiana@la | Gelotiana
details: The domus is the findspot of the so-called "Alexamenos graffito".
description: A domus on the slope of the Palatine Hill that Caius incorporated into the Imperial Palace complex.

title: Thermae Novati | Thermae Novatianae
name_variants: Thermae Novati@la | Thermae Novatianae@la | Thermae Novati | Thermae Novatianae
description: Thermae Novati, ancient baths of the Vicus Patricius that were located in the vicinity of S. Pudenziana.

title: Calippe
name_variants: Calippe@la | Calippe
description: A place in India included on the Peutinger map.

title: Templum lovis optimi maximi
name_variants: Tempio esastilo nel Foro@it | Tempio o Basilica di Giove@it | Temple of Jupiter@en | Erario@it | Erario pubblico@it | Tesoro@it | Tempio di Venere Fisica Pompeiana@it | Tempio della triade Capitolina@it | Tempio di Giove@it | Senaculum@la | Curia@la | Aerarium@la | Templum lovis optimi maximi@la | Templum of Jupiter@en | Capitolium@la | VII.8.1@en | Tempio esastilo nel Foro | Tempio o Basilica di Giove | Temple of Jupiter | Erario | Erario pubblico | Tesoro | Tempio di Venere Fisica Pompeiana | Tempio della triade Capitolina | Tempio di Giove | Giunone e Minerva | Senaculum | Curia | Aerarium | Templum lovis opt. max. | Templum of Jupiter | Ceres et Venus Pompeiana | Capitolium | VII.8.1 | Templum lovis optimi maximi
description: The Temple of Jupiter (VII,8,1) in Pompeii sits at the north end of the forum. It was built in the middle of the second century BC.

title: Ianus Quadrifons
name_variants: Ianus Quadrifons@la | Arch of Janus@en | Ianus Quadrifons | Arch of Janus | Ianus Quadrifons
description: A quadrifrons triumphal arch at Rome that is located at a crossroads in the area of the Velabrum and the Forum Boarium. It dates to the early fourth century AD; its construction employed spolia, and it likely honored either Constantine I or Constantius II.

title: Almo
name_variants: Almo@la | Almo
description: A small river of the Ager Romanus that once joined the Tiber River just below the walls of Rome. Almo, the eldest son of Tyrrhus, who is one of the heroes in Virgil's Aeneid, shares the river's name.

title: Albanus ager
name_variants: Albanus ager@la | Albanus ager
description: A famously fertile territory of central Italy that originally was a part of Alba Longa. This region lay between the lacus Albanus, Bovillae, and Aricia. The Roman Via Appia passed through it.

title: Tellurenses
name_variants: Tellurenses@la | Tellurenses
description: A Latin inscription of ca. 375 CE mentions the Tellurenses, namely people living in the district of the Temple of Tellus at Rome.

title: Simiati
name_variants: Simiati@la | Simiati
description: Simiati is a place included in the Peutinger map. It was located in the eastern part of the Nile River Delta.

title: Horti Maiani
name_variants: Horti Maiani@la | Horti Maiani
description: An urban garden of imperial Rome located on the summit of the Esquiline Hill. Based on an inscription dating to the reign of Claudius, it is believed that these gardens were administered by the same magistrate in charge of the Horti Lamiani, an official with the title "procurator hortorum Maianorum et Lamianorum".

title: aedes Salutis
name_variants: aedes Salutis@la | aedes Salutis
description: While consul in 311 BCE, Caius Iunius Bubulcus Brutus vowed the temple of Salus; he would later dedicate it as dictator in 302 BCE. While no physical remains of the temple are known, textual and epigraphic testimony suggest that it would have been located near the present-day Piazza del Quirinale.

title: Campus Viminalis
name_variants: Campus Viminalis@la | Campus Viminalis
description: An open area on the Esquiline Hill that is mentioned in the Regionary Catalogues for Regio V. It was likely a narrow area that lay outside the so-called Servian Wall.

title: Tuscus vicus | Vicus Turarius
name_variants: Tuscus vicus@la | Vicus Turarius@la | Vicus Tuscus | Vicus Turarius | Tuscus vicus | Vicus Turarius

details: Construction of the Forum Iulium began in 54 B.C., and it was dedicated in 46 B.C. upon its completion. As part of the dedication, lavish games were also offered and funded by Caesar, indicating the staggering amount that he personally invested in the project. The Forum Iulium measured 160 meters by 75 meters, reaching from the Argiletum on the southeast side of the Forum Romanum to the Atrium Libertatis . The Forum of Caesar was originally meant to be an expansion of the Forum Romanum. The Forum, however, evolved so that it served two additional purposes. As Caesar became more and more involved in this project, the Forum became a place for public business that was related to the Senate in addition to a shrine for himself as well as Venus Genetrix . The large temple was originally planned to be dedicated to Venus Victrix. Following his victory at Pharsalus, Caesar decided to honor Venus Genetrix , the goddess of motherhood and domesticity, instead. He believed this deity to be the origin of the gens Iulia to which he belonged. The forum was heavily damaged in the widespread fires of A.D. 80 and did not see reconstruction until ca. A.D. 95-100 under the reigns of Domitian and Trajan, respectively.

The statue was originally an element of the sprawling Domus Aurea of Nero but the monument endured long after Nero's reign. The statue's original position likely marked the summit of the Velian Hill. The Flavians refashioned the statue to resemble Sol and Hadrian relocated the statue nearer the Flavian amphitheater as part of the work to create the Temple of Venus and Roma.

title: sororium tigillum
name_variants: sororium tigillum@la | sororium tigillum
description: Sororium Tigillum describes a wooden beam that stretched across a branch of the Sacra Via that climbed the Oppian Hill near the Compitum Acilii. The monument was flanked by altars of Iuno Sororia and Iuno Curiatius. It is an ancient monument about which there are many stories, the primary one being a link to the Horatii and Curiatii and Publius Horatius' slaying of his own sister.

title: Protesilai Sepulchrum
name_variants: Protesilai Sepulchrum@la | Πρωτεσίλεω τάφος@grc | Protesilai Sepulchrum | Protesileo taphos | Protesilai Sepulchrum
description: Tomb of the mythic figure Protesilaus, first to die in the Trojan War. According to ancient testimony, the tomb was located on the Chersonesus, near Elaeus, its precise location is not known today.

title: Vicus Iudaeorum
name_variants: Vicus Iudaeorum@la | Vicus Iudaeorum
details: According to G. Beer (RE: Vicus Iudaeorum), the place should be distinguished from Castra Iudaeorum mentioned in Notitia Dignitatum. In Trismegistos, however, the two are considered the same place.
description: A place in Lower Egypt on the eastern bank of the Nile River, mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary. Possibly located in the vicinity of Bubastis.

title: via Pedana
name_variants: via Pedana@la | via Pedana
description: The via Pedana, known only from epigraphic evidence, led presumably from Rome to Pedum. It was likely a branch of the via Praenestina.

title: regio Pedana
name_variants: regio Pedana@la | regio Pedana
description: The territory of the city of Pedum, referred to as both "regio Pedana" and "ager Pedanus" was known to Cicero and Horace but all traces had vanished by the time of Pliny the Elder.

title: portus Mossylites
name_variants: portus Mossylites@la | portus Mossylites
description: A port located in east Africa, some two to three days' journey to the east of the ancient island of Mundu.

title: Ager Faliscus
name_variants: Ager Faliscus@la | Ager Faliscus
description: The territory of the Faliscans that lay between areas where Etruscan, Latin, and Sabellic languages were spoken. The geographic limits of this territory on the right bank of the Tiber River stretch from Grotta Porciosa in the north to Capena in the south.

title: Falerna
name_variants: Falerna@la | Falerna
details: The tribus Falerna was assigned to the Ager Falernus after 338 B.C.
description: A rural tribe of Rome, which was established in 318 B.C.

title: Titulus Vestinae
name_variants: Titulus Vestinae@la | Titulus Vestinae
description: The basilica of Saints Vitalis, Valeris, Gervase, and Protase, commonly known as the Basilica di San Vitale, is a titular minor basilica church in Rome. The church was built ca. AD 400 by Pope Innocent I.

title: Dagae
name_variants: Dagae@la | Dagae
description: An ethnic name in Dacia included on the Peutinger map.

title: Amphitheatrum Castrense

title: Via Aurelia
name_variants: Via Aurelia@la | Via Aurelia
description: A Roman road.

description: A river included on the Peutinger map.

title: Abaesamis

description: Pliny the Elder mentions a settlement called Abaesamis located in Arabia Petraea.

title: XATIS SCYTHAE
name_variants: XATIS SCYTHAE@la | Xatis Scythae | XATIS SCYTHAE
description: Xati Scythae, an ancient people of the Roman Empire.

description: The Basilica Porcia is considered the first named civil basilica in Rome. The elder Cato is responsible for its construction in 184 BCE. It seems to have been a small structure that took the place of several earlier private atria located between the Clivus Argentarius and the Curia Hostilia. The Basilica Porcia was destroyed by fire in 52 BCE.

title: Mucionis | Mugionia porta

description: The Porta Mugonia was one of the three gates of the original Palatine city of Rome (often referred to as "Roma quadrata"). Its precise location can no longer be established and it remains a hotly debated issue for topographers.

title: Via Claudia Valeria
name_variants: Via Claudia Valeria@la | Via Claudia Valeria
description: A portion of the Via Valeria connecting Aternum and Corfinium. A Claudian milestone (CIL 9.5973) records the construction taking place in AD 48/9 and that the road ran from Cerfennia to the mouth of the Aternus river (modern Pescara).

title: Alonianv̄
name_variants: Alonianv̄@la | Alonianum | Alonianv̄
description: Alonianum was a place in Africa that is included on the Peutinger map. It is likely a road station positioned along the way from Thelepte to Tacapae via the palus Tritonis.

title: Regia
name_variants: Regia@la | Regia
description: The Regia is an ancient complex along the Sacra Via in Rome at the margin of the Forum Romanum, adjacent to the Temple of Vesta. It is understood as a sort of ritual headquarters of Rome's early kings and, later, as a structure connected with the office of the pontifex maximus.

title: Vicus Sulpicius
name_variants: Vicus Sulpicius@la | Vicus Sulpicius
description: A street in ancient Rome that is mentioned on the so-called Capitoline Base (CIL 6, 975).

title: Aqvas volaternas
name_variants: Aqvas volaternas@la | Aquas volaternas | Aqvas volaternas
description: A place named on the Peutinger map, possibly to be associated with modern Monte Cerboli, Italy.

title: Caleorsissa
name_variants: Caleorsissa@la | Caleorsissa
description: An ancient place in Cappadocia located on the route between Olotoedariza and Analib(l)a.

title: Tromentina
name_variants: Tromentina@la | Tromentina
details: With the fall of Veii in 396 B.C., the Veientine territory passed into Roman control and four new tribes were organised. The tribus Tromentina was among the new tribes and it was established at the site of Veii.
description: A later rural tribe of ancient Rome, which was established in 387 B.C.

title: Byrsa
name_variants: Βύρσα@grc | Byrsa@en | Byrsa@la | Byrsa
description: Walled citadel in Carthage built in the early first millennium BCE. The site was destroyed during the Third Punic War in 146 BCE by the forces of Scipio Aemilianus. The hill became the site of the city's forum in the Roman period.

title: Lacus pastorum
name_variants: Lacus pastorum@la | Lacus pastorum
description: A place in Regio III, likely located to the south of the Baths of Trajan.

title: Elephas herbarius | elefantum herbarium
name_variants: Elephas herbarius@la | elefantum herbarium@la | Elephas herbarius | elefantum herbarium
details: A church that is known in the eighth century, one "Abbacyrus ad Alaphantum", might lead us to conclude that the elephant is to be located nearer the Tiber banks, not far from S. Nicola in Carcere.
description: Elephas herbarius (Elefantum herbarium), a place included in the Notitia, is mentioned only once and must lie at the southern limit of Regio VIII. Coarelli concludes that this place must have been located on the lower slopes of the Capitoline Hill facing the Forum Holitorium. Its coincidence with Late Antique and Medieval toponyms suggests that it refers to an ancient statue of an elephant, perhaps one shown eating plants, in the area of the Forum Holitorium.

title: Domus Flavia
name_variants: Domus Flavia@la | Domus Flavia
description: The Domus Flavia is a modern appellation that refers to the palace complex built by the emperor Domitian on the Palatine Hill in Rome. The complex was completed ca. 92 CE. The Flavian complex is considered a part of the larger entity known as Domus Palatina.

title: Lupercal
name_variants: Lupercal@la | Lupercal
description: A cave located at the foot of the Palatine Hill in Rome in which the she-wolf was said to have been found suckling the twins, Romulus and Remus.

title: Forum | Ludus gladiatorius | Schola gladiatoria | Castrum militum

title: Porticus margaritaria
name_variants: Porticus margaritaria@la | Porticus margaritaria
description: A place located in regio VIII that was connected with jewelers. While the porticus itself is mentioned only in the Regionary Catalogues, numerous extant inscriptions attest to the shops of jewelers in the vicinity of the Sacra Via.

title: Forum Suarium
name_variants: Forum Suarium@la | Forum Suarium
description: A forum venalium of ancient Rome linked to the sale of pork, the Forum Suarium is mentioned in two inscriptions dating ca. 200 CE. The forum lay near the barracks of the urban cohorts (cohortes urbanae) in the northern portion of the Campus Martius, perhaps near the location of the present Via di Propaganda in metropolitan Rome.

title: gens Claudia
name_variants: gens Claudia@la | gens Claudia
details: The Claudia tribe was organised in 504 B.C. by the founder of the Claudian house Attius Clausus, later known as Appius Claudius. It was located north of Anio, between Fidenae and Ficulea. Later Claudia adjoined with Clustumina tribe.
description: A Roman rural tribe that was one of the most ancient of Rome's gentes. The gens Claudia traced its history to the earliest days of the Roman Republic. Appius Claudius Sabinus Regillensis, in 495 B.C., was the first of its members to hold the consulship.

title: Amiternum
name_variants: Amiternum@la | Amiternum
details: During the Third Samnite War (293 B.C.), the Roman consul Spurius Carvilius Maximus captured and destroyed Amiternum. The opinion offered by S. Oakley contradicts those of Nissen, Salmon, and La Regina.
description: An ancient city in Samnium, located between Interamna Lirenas and Atina, perhaps corresponding to the modern comune of Sant'Elia Fiumerapido (FR).

title: Lichades
name_variants: Lichades@la | Λιχάδες@grc | Lichades
description: An island group off North Euboea, Greece. Near the Malian Gulf.

title: vici Luccei
name_variants: vici Luccei@la | vici Luccei
description: Buildings in the Forum Boarium, mentioned by Cicero, that correspond to a Latin inscription discovered in 1939 and published by Silvio Panciera in 1970.

title: Regio IX
name_variants: Regio IX@la | Regio IX
description: One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Liguria. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.

title: Caprae palus
name_variants: Caprae palus@la | Αἰγὸς ἕλος@grc | Caprae palus | Aigos Helos | Caprae palus
description: A site in the Campus Martius of Rome where mytho-historic tradition held that Romulus vanished during a storm, thus marking his apotheosis.

title: insula Batavorum
name_variants: insula Batavorum@la | Insula Batavorum | insula Batavorum
description: Both Iulius Caesar and Tacitus refer to the "Island of the Batavi", once located at a split in the Rhine and framed by the Waal river on the one hand and the Lower Rhine on the other. This area seems to correspond roughly to the modern Betuwe in the Netherlands.

title: tribus Stellatina
name_variants: tribus Stellatina@la | Stellatina | tribus Stellatina
details: The tribus Stellatina was located to the northeast of Rome, towards the Tiber river. It later became the tribe of Capena.
description: The tribus Stellatina was a later rural tribe of ancient Rome which was established in 387 B.C.

title: sacellum Streniae
name_variants: sacellum Streniae@la | sacellum Streniae
description: The Shrine of Strenia was located in the valley of the Colosseum and is mentioned as the starting point of the Sacra Via.

title: Schola Praeconum
name_variants: Schola Praeconum@la | Scuola degli Araldi@it | Schola Praeconum | Scuola degli Araldi | Schola Praeconum
description: The so-called Schola Praeconum is located at the foot of the Palatine Hill near the church of S. Anastasia. A black-and-white floor mosaic discovered during excavations depicts public heralds known as praecones, thus the name of the site.

title: Cassiterides
name_variants: Κασσιτερίδας@grc | Cassiterides@la | Καττιτερίδες@grc | Kassiteridas | Cassiterides | Kattiterides | Cassiterides
description: An unlocatable group of islands somewhere off the Atlantic European coast, said by ancient authors to be a source of tin. This name may constitute an early, vague generalization concerning multiple islands and coastal areas of Gaul and Britain.

title: via Ardeatina
name_variants: via Ardeatina@la | Via Ardeatina | via Ardeatina
description: The Via Ardeatina connected Rome and Ardea.

title: Monumentum Antiochenum
name_variants: Monumentum Antiochenum@la | Monumentum Antiochenum
description: The Augusteum, or Sebasteion, at Antioch in Pisidia was a monumental architectural complex dedicated to the Roman Imperial cult. Its archaeological remains were first excavated in 1913. Approximately 60 fragments of the Res Gestae Divi Augusti were discovered at the site.

title: Porta Metronia
name_variants: Porta Metronia@la | Porta Metronia
description: Porta Metronia, a gate in the Aurelian Walls of Rome.

title: Porta Portuensis
name_variants: Porta Portese@it | Porta Portuensis@la | Porta Portese | Porta Portuensis | Porta Portuensis
description: The Porta Portuensis was one of the gates of the Aurelian Wall of Rome, located in the Transtiberim. The original gate carried an inscription of Honorius and was destroyed during the reign of Pope Urban VIII. The present Porta Portese, built by architect Vincenzo Maculani in 1644, occupies its site.

title: Ludus Magnus
name_variants: Ludus Magnus@la | Ludus Magnus
description: A gladiatorial training school adjacent to the Flavian Amphitheater in Rome. The structure is attested on the Severan marble plan of Rome.

title: Regio VII
name_variants: Regio VII@la | Regio VII
details: The perimeter of the region was approximately 4.64 km or 15,700 Roman feet.
description: Regio VII (Via Lata) was one of the administrative regions of the city of Rome instituted by Augustus in 7 BCE. In addition to the named monuments and buildings, the Regionary Catalogues indicate that this district also included 15 shrines (aediculae), 120 townhouses (domūs), 25 warehouses (horrea), 75 baths (balneae), and 76 fountains.

title: Sarabodis uilla

description: Roman villa rustica

title: Petronia amnis

description: A brook in the Campus Martius of ancient Rome that flowed from the Cati fons to the Tiber River.

title: ager Romanus

description: The rural hinterland of the ancient city of Rome.

title: Fufidianum
name_variants: Fufidianum@la | Fufidianum

title: Fines

title: Thasarte
name_variants: Thasarte@la | Thasarte
description: Now unlocated, Thasarte was a place in Africa Proconsularis that is included on the Peutinger map.

title: Anami
name_variants: Anami@la | Anami
description: Anami was an ancient settlement in Egypt. It is marked on the Peutinger map along the route leading from Panopolis to Chenoboskeion. Anami was not included in the Barrington Atlas. It should be noted that compilers of the Tabula Peutingeriana database at the Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt correlate Anami with a place named Antaiopolis/Tkoou (BAtlas 77 FC) that is a standalone place in the Pleiades gazetteer.

title: Aeaea
name_variants: Αιαία@grc | Aeaea@la | Aiaia | Aeaea | Aeaea
description: The mythical, unlocatable island of Circe from the Odyssey, visited by Odysseus. Possibly identified with Cape Circaion on the west coast of Italy

title: Myrmeces scopuli
name_variants: Myrmeces scopuli@la | Myrmeces scopuli
description: Myrmeces scopuli, cliffs or rocks near the mouth of the Hermos River at the point where it debouches into the Gulf of Smyrna. According to Pliny the Elder, they are to be located near Leukai.

title: Praenestina via
