description: A consular road running from Rome to Praeneste.

title: balneum Caesaris
name_variants: balneum Caesaris@la | balneum Caesaris
description: A bath complex known from the Severan marble plan and perhaps also referred to in the Historia Augusta.

title: Eumenetica
name_variants: Eumenetica@la | Eumenetica
description: An ancient region located on the border of Lydia and Phrygia through which the Meander river flowed.

title: Basilica Ulpia
name_variants: Basilica Ulpia@la | Basilica Ulpia
description: The Basilica Ulpia is located in the Forum of Trajan at Rome and derives its name from the emperor Trajan's gentilician nomenclature. The basilica was considered a marvel of ancient Roman architecture by observers, including the historian Ammianus Marcellinus.

title: Ciphris
name_variants: Κίρφις@grc | Ciphris@la | Kirphis | Cirphis | Ciphris
description: Mountain in central Greece, south of Delphi.

title: Graecostadium
name_variants: Graecostadium@la | Graecostadium
description: Located in Regio VIII of the ancient city of Rome, Graecostadium refers to a place that is either an area that is enclosed by walls or a set of buildings. This seems to have been a large area in any case. The Graecostadium is damaged by fire and subsequently restored under Antoninus Pius. Ths place burned again during the reign of Carinus.

title: VMBRANICIA
name_variants: VMBRANICIA@la | Umbranicia | VMBRANICIA
description: A region in Gaul marked on the Peutinger map.

title: Via Hadriana
name_variants: Via Hadriana@la | Via Hadriana
description: A Roman road established by Hadrian running from Antinoopolis to Berenice. The road was completed in AD 137.

title: porticus Eventus Boni
name_variants: porticus Eventus Boni@la | porticus Eventus Boni
description: A portico built in 374 CE by an urban prefect named Claudius near the temple of the god Bonus Eventus.

title: Fortunae huiusce [d]iei in campo | aedes Catuli

title: Fines cilicie

description: A place attested on the Tabula Peutingeriana, located along the route between Lagania and Balgatia. Talbert notes that there is some uncertainty about the name and posits that the copyist could have made an error.

title: Tities
name_variants: Tities@la | Tities

title: Cutilia
name_variants: Cutilia@la | Cutilia
description: A Sabine town located between Reate and Interocrium.

title: Ad stabvlvm
name_variants: Ad stabvlvm@la | Ad stabulum | Ad stabvlvm
description: A road station in Pontus along the Roman road from Zela to Neokaisareia.

title: Flavia marci | Falavi Marci
name_variants: Flavia marci@la | Falavi Marci@la | Flavia marci | Falavi Marci
description: An unlocated place in ancient Numidia, Flavia marci was situated some 47 Roman miles from Theveste along the road leading to Cirta.

title: templum divi Claudii
name_variants: templum divi Claudii@la | Temple of Claudius@en | templum divi Claudii | Temple of Claudius | templum divi Claudii
description: A temple dedicated to the emperor Claudius who was declared divus (deified) after his death in 54 CE. The platform temple occupied a large area of the Caelian Hill in Rome. The construction project was ultimately completed by the Flavians.

title: Aequimelium
name_variants: Aequimelium@la | Aequimelium
description: The Aequimelium was an open area on the southeast slope of the Capitoline Hill. This space may have once been the site of the house of one Spurius Maelius, a Roman citizen of the fifth century BCE who was slain for the crime of wanting to be a king (adfectatio regni).

title: Campus Agrippae
name_variants: Campus Agrippae@la | Campus Agrippae
details: According to Cassius Dio, Augustus donated this area to the Roman people in 7 BCE. It lies to the right of the via Flaminia and to the north of the line of the aqua Virgo. From 38 CE, it was the site of the ara Providentiae.
description: "Campus Agrippae" describes an area within regio VII of ancient Rome that is connected to the building activities of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa in the first century BCE.

title: Ferresanus Portus
name_variants: Ferresanus Portus@la | Ferresanus Portus
description: A Roman military harbor facility, attested by name in a Latin inscription dating to 144 CE, on the island of Farasan in the Red Sea. The exact location of the facility is not known; the inscription was found in a context of reuse.

title: Hercynna
name_variants: Ἕρκυνα@grc | Hercynna@la | Herkyna | Hercynna | Hercynna
description: A river in Boeotia that flows through Livadeia.

title: Tribono
name_variants: Tribono@la | Tribonum | Tribono
details: The estate was confirmed as possession of the bishoprics of Cologne and Metz by king Sigebert III in 640/647. In the charter Tribonum is said to have belonged to queen Brunhilda (d. 613) and later king Clotaire II (d. 614) and Dagobert I (d. 639).
description: An estate formely belonging to Queen Brunhilda, daugther of the Visigoth king Athanagild and married to king Sigebert I

title: Porta Appia
name_variants: Porta Appia@la | Porta San Sebastiano@it | Porta Appia | Porta San Sebastiano | Porta Appia
description: A gate in the Aurelian Wall through which the Via Appia passed. Now known as Porta S. Sebastiano.

title: Vicus Veneris Almae
name_variants: Vicus Veneris Almae@la | Vicus Veneris Almae
description: A street in Regio XII of ancient Rome that is also listed on the so-called Capitoline Base. It may have been located southeast of the Circus Maximus.

title: Coccium
name_variants: Coccium@la | Coccium
description: A minor Romano-British settlement located at Wigan, Lancashire.

title: Palsicium
name_variants: Palsicium@la | Palsicium
description: A one-time coastal settlement of the Veneti in northern Italy that Pliny the Elder records as having disappeared before his time.

title: fossa Cluilia
name_variants: fossa Cluilia@la | fossa Cluilia
description: The Fossa Cluilia was a defensive ditch built by Caius Cluilius, king of Alba Longa, during Alba Longa's war with Rome in the seventh century B.C.

title: Pupinia tribus
name_variants: Pupinia tribus@la | Pupinia tribus
description: The tribus Pupinia was one of the oldest rural tribes of ancient Rome. Festus indicates that its name is derived from an area lying between Tusculum and Rome.

title: Hadrianeum | templum Hadriani
name_variants: Temple of Hadrian@en | Hadrianeum@la | templum Hadriani@la | Temple of Hadrian | Hadrianeum | templum Hadriani | Hadrianeum | templum Hadriani
description: The Temple of Hadrian at Rome, also referred to as the Hadrianeum, was a temple located in the Campus Martius dedicated to the deified Hadrian by Antoninus Pius in 145 CE. Some of the temple's substantial remains were incorporated into a 17th-century building designed by architect Carlo Fontana in Rome's Piazza di Pietra.

title: Reccopolis
name_variants: Recópolis@es | Reccopolis@la | Recópolis | Reccopolis | Reccopolis
description: Reccopolis is an urban, Visigothic, ex-novo foundation made under king Liuvigild in A.D. 578. The archaeological remains at the site include a palace complex, public area, basilica, walls, and aqueduct. The site is known today by the Spanish version of its Latin name (Recópolis); it is located near the modern village of Zorita de los Canes in the Spanish province of Guadelajara.

title: Flenio
name_variants: Flenio@la | Flenio
description: Flenium was a statio incuded on the Peutinger map. It was located between Forum Hadriani and Tablae in the territory of the Batavians. Its location is unknown.

title: tabernae circa forum
name_variants: tabernae circa forum@la | tabernae circa forum
description: Shops surrounding the early Forum Romanum. Tradition assigns their construction to Tarquinius Priscus.

title: Tasgoduni
name_variants: Tasgoduni@la | Tasgoduni
description: An ancient tribe of Gallia Narbonensis.

title: Acanthus
name_variants: Acanthus@la | Acanthus
description: Acanthus is an island in the Propontis named by Pliny the Elder.

title: sacrum Cloacina
name_variants: sacrum Cloacina@la | sacrum Cloacina
description: The Sacrum Cloacina was a small shrine dedicated to Venus Cloacina, patron divinity of the sewer, and was located near the Tabernae novae in the Forum Romanum. The foundation of the sacellum is extant while images of its likely elevation are found on Roman coins.

title: Incomacenis
name_variants: Incomacenis@la | Incomacenis
description: A place included on the Peutinger map.

title: Basilica Nova | Basilica Constantini
name_variants: Basilica Nova@la | Basilica of Maxentius@en | Basilica Constantini@la | Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine@en | Basilica di Massenzio@it | Basilika des Maxentius und Konstantin@de | Basilica di Constantino@it | Basilica Nova | Basilica of Maxentius | Basilica Constantini | Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine | Basilica di Massenzio | Basilika des Maxentius und Konstantin | Basilica di Constantino | Basilica Nova | Basilica Constantini
details: The project began in 308 CE under the emperor Maxentius but was completed by Constantine I in 312 after his victory over Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge. A rectangular platform (328 by 213 feet) supports the structure. The central nave of the basilica measures 80 m (260 ft) long, 25 m (82 ft) wide, and 35 m (115 ft) high, while the side aisles measure 16 m (52 ft) wide and 24.5 m (80 ft) high.
description: The Basilica Constantini, also called Basilica Nova ("New Basilica"), Basilica of Maxentius, or Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine, is a colossal fourth-century basilica along the Sacra Via in Rome. It is considered the largest ancient structure in the valley of the Forum Romanum and is often regarded as the final Roman civic basilica built in the ancient city.

title: Fundus Campus Naranus
name_variants: Fundus Campus Naranus@la | Fundus Campus Naranus
description: Fundus Campus Naranus, a region located near Volcei in Bruttium et Lucania (Regio III).

title: Esquilinae
name_variants: Esquilinae@la | Collis Aesquilinus@la | Esquilinae | Collis Aesquilinus | Esquilinae
description: The Esquiline Hill is one of the seven hills of Rome. The eastern section of the hill lay outside the Servian Wall, and served as a pauper's cemetery during the archaic and Republican periods.

title: balineum Bolani
name_variants: balineum Bolani@la | balineum Bolani
description: A bath complex mentioned only in the regionary catalog for regio I of ancient Rome. Its patron may have been M. Vettius Bolanus (suffect consul in 66 CE), the same individual known for property holdings in Trastevere.

title: Via Claudia Augusta
name_variants: Via Claudia Augusta@la | Via Claudia Augusta
details: The Barrington Atlas Directory for map 12 notes that the "Via Claudia Augusta is the only named road known in the area of the map. It runs from the Po valley over the Alps, into the Alpine foothills in Bavaria, and on to the Danube."
description: The Via Claudia Augusta was a Roman road that traversed the Alps, connecting the Po River valley to Rhaetia. Claudius began its construction in AD 46/7.

title: Via Amerina
name_variants: Via Amerina@la | Via Amerina
description: A Roman road begun ca. 241 B.C. that connected Veii and Ameria.

title: Aquae Labanae
name_variants: τὰ Λαβανὰ ὕδατα@grc | Aquae Labanae@la | ta Labana udata | Aquae Labanae | Aquae Labanae
description: Cold, sulfur springs located near Nomentum, according to Strabo.

title: aedes Concordiae
name_variants: Temple of Concord@en | aedes Concordiae@la | Temple of Concord | aedes Concordiae | aedes Concordiae
description: The Temple of Concord at Rome was located at the western margin of the Forum Romanum. Its origins are sometimes linked to a vow made by Marcus Furius Camillus in 367 BCE, but the vow may not have been fulfilled until 218 BCE under Lucius Manlius. The sanctuary was rebuilt in 121 BCE and again in 10 CE.

title: Caelius mons
name_variants: Caelius mons@la | Caelian Hill@en | τὸ Καίλιον ὄρος@grc | Monte Celio@it | Caelius Mons | Caelian Hill | to Kailion oros | Monte Celio | Caelius mons
details: The Caelian Hill, measuring approximately 2 km in length and with an elevation of 500 meters, is counted as one of Rome's hills, although a good portion of the hill lies outside the bounds of the pomerium . During the Republican period the hill was still used for burials but by the Imperial period the Caelian had become a fashionable residential quarter. During the first century AD the Caelian was chosen to be the site of a monumental platform temple dedicated to the deified emperor Claudius ( divus Claudius ). This project went through several phases, being interrupted under Nero who transformed it into a nymphaeum. The project was completed under the administration of the Flavians.
description: The Caelian Hill in Rome.

title: Porta Praenestina
name_variants: Porta Praenestina@la | Porta Maggiore@it | Porta Praenestina | Porta Maggiore | Porta Praenestina
description: The Porta Maggiore is the ancient Porta Praenestina, an early Imperial gate preserved in the later third century walls built by Aurelian.

title: murus romuli
name_variants: murus romuli@la | τεῖχος Ῥωμύλου@grc | murus romuli | teichos Romulou | murus romuli
description: "Murus Romuli" refers to a fortification wall alleged to have surrounded the Palatine Hill in Rome, Italy. Legendary tradition claims it was built by the founder-hero Romulus during the eighth century BCE. The historicity of the wall remains hotly debated.

title: Via Nomentana | Via Nvmentana
name_variants: Via Nomentana@la | Νωμεντανή (ἡ)@grc | Via Nvmentana@la | Via Nomentana | Uia Nomentana | Nomentane | Nomentanē | Via Numentana | Via Nomentana | Via Nvmentana
description: The ancient road connecting Rome and Nomentum.

title: aedis Martis
name_variants: aedis Martis@la | aedis Martis
description: A temple sacred to Mars located on the Via Appia. The shrine was located between the first and second milestones and was dedicated in the fourth century BC. According to Livy, Titus Quinctius dedicated the temple on 1 June 387 BC.

title: Regio VI
name_variants: Regio VI@la | Regio VI
description: One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Umbria and Ager Gallicus. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.

title: Regio VII
name_variants: Regio VII@la | Regio VII
description: One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Etruria. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.

title: Sepulcrum Pansae
name_variants: Sepulcrum Pansae@la | Sepulcrum Pansae
description: The tomb of the consul Gaius Vibius Pansa Caetronianus (43 B.C.) was located in the Campus Martius of Rome according to both literary and epigraphic testimony. Its precise location has not been determined.

title: Rogmor(vm)
name_variants: Rogmor(vm)@la | Rogmorum | Rogmor(vm)
description: Rogmorum is a toponym included on the Peutinger map, and it is connected to roadways radiating from Tavium toward the east. Wilson discusses whether or not Rogmorum is a corruption of Trocmorum, an epithet connected with Tavium. The compilers of the Barrington Atlas did not include this place on map 63.

title: Oufentina
name_variants: Oufentina@la | Oufentina
details: The name of tribus Oufentina derives from the river Ufens and was in the territory of Privernum.
description: The tribus Oufentina was a later rural tribe of Rome, established in 318 B.C.

title: lacus qui vocatur Ianula
name_variants: lacus qui vocatur Ianula@la | Lacus Ianula | lacus qui vocatur Ianula
description: A volcanic crater lake located near Viterbo, Italy. The study of lacustrine sediments has revealed palynological evidence that has helped to reconstruct the ancient environment and vegetation of peninsular Italy.

title: conventus Astigitanus
name_variants: conventus Astigitanus@la | conventus Astigitanus
description: An administrative subdivision of Roman Baetica.

title: Ulubrenses | Vlubrae
name_variants: Ulubrenses@la | Vlubrae@la | Ulubrenses | Ulubrae | Ulubrenses | Vlubrae
description: An ancient settlement of Latium located near the Pontine Marshes.

title: Ad Cazalis | Adcahalis
name_variants: Ad Cazalis@la | Adcahalis@la | Ad Cazalis | Adcahalis
description: Ad Cahalis (or Ad Cazalis) was a road station in ancient Numidia. It was located along the road from Theveste to Thamugas.

title: Septemzodium | Sept[izod]ium | Septisolium
name_variants: Septizonium@la | Septemzodium@la | Sept[izod]ium@la | Septisolium@la | Settizonio@it | Septizonium | Septemzodium | Septizodium | Septisolium | Settizonio | Septemzodium | Sept[izod]ium | Septisolium
details: The Septizonium was a five-story monument incorporating exedrae, inspired by theatrical architecture. It may have served as a monumental fountain or nymphaeum. Its topographical placement at the intersection of the Via Triumphalis and the Via Appia may have been part of a Severan re-focusing of Rome's topography. The monument is attested on the Severan Marble Plan (a.k.a. Forma Urbis Romae ) and is featured in several early modern accounts of the monuments of ancient Rome, including Étienne Dupérac's accounting ca. 1575.
description: The Septizonium (or Septizodium) is a monument located at the extreme southeastern corner of the Palatine Hill, built by the Severan emperors. It is attested to textually in the Historia Augusta; its footprint is visible on the Severan marble plan (Forma Urbis Romae), and its foundations have been explored through excavation.

title: Casae
name_variants: Henchir-el-Beguar@en | Henchir El Begar 1@fr | Casae@la | Henchir-el-Beguar | Henchir El Begar 1 | Casae | Casae
description: Modern Henchir el Beguar/Begar, an archaeological site located in the Tunisian governorate of Kasserine. Inscriptions of the second century CE found here in the 19th century authorized the holding of regular markets at Casae and demonstrate that it was probably the principal settlement of the Saltus Beguensis, a Roman senatorial estate.

title: lacus Iuturnae
name_variants: lacus Iuturnae@la | Lacus Iuturnae | lacus Iuturnae
description: The Lacus Iuturnae was a pool built near a spring sacred to Iuturna. Legend held that the Dioscuri watered their horses there after the Battle of Lake Regillus in 495 BCE.

title: Basilica Hilariana
name_variants: Basilica Hilariana@la | Basilica Hilariana
description: A basilica erected on the Caelian Hill in Rome under the patronage of Manius Publicus Hilarus and connected to the cult of Cybele and Attis.

title: Ad dvodecimvm
name_variants: Ad dvodecimvm@la | Ad Duodecimum | Ad dvodecimvm
description: A station (statio) located in the territory of the Batavians between Grinnes and Noviomagus.

title: Numinienses
name_variants: Numinienses@la | Numinienses
description: One of the lost peoples of Latium as enumerated by Pliny the Elder.

title: Fidenates
name_variants: Fidenates@la | Fidenates
details: R.E.A Palmer stresses that these Fidenates are to be considered separately from the people of Fidenae .
description: The Fidenates number among the lost peoples of Latium enumerated by Pliny the Elder.

title: Dratinus
name_variants: Dratinus@la | Dratinus
description: A river that Pliny the Elder describes as flowing into the Persian Gulf.

title: Thapedon
name_variants: Thapedon@la | Thapedon
description: A place included on the Peutinger map.

title: Porticus Vipsania
name_variants: Porticus Vipsania@la | Porticus Vipsania
description: The Porticus Vipsania was a public complex located along the eastern side of the via Lata in the Campus Martius. This complex contained a map commissioned by Agrippa. The project was begun under Polla (Agrippa's sister) and completed under Augustus.

title: Arcus Novus
name_variants: Arcus Novus@la | Arcus Novus
details: The Arcus Novus relied on reused sculptural reliefs ( spolia ) that likely were taken from the Ara Pietatis. Elements of the nearby Temple of the Sun were also perhaps coopted. By order of Innocent VIII, the arch was demolished in 1491. Fragments of relief sculpture were discovered in 1523 and eventually passed into the ownership of the Medici family, with some fragments making their way to the Boboli Gardens in Florence, Italy. The Diocletianic arch also reused relief sculpture from the Antonine period. These fragments also came to be owned by the Medici and were incorporated into the facade of the Villa Medici in Rome.
description: A now-lost arch on the ancient Via Lata. It was dedicated to Diocletian either in 293 CE (marking the occasion of his decennalia) or in 303-304 (joint triumph with Maximian). The present church of Santa Maria in Via Lata occupies the site of the arch.

title: Egelestani
name_variants: Egelestani@la | Egelestani
details: Pedro Barceló argues, in New Pauly , that claims that Egelasta should be taken as equivalent to Iniesta are mistaken.
description: An ancient settlement in Iberia that was part of the conventus of Carthago Nova, according to Pliny the Elder. It is noted in particular for its salt.

title: Thimara
name_variants: Thimara@la | Thimara
description: A place in south Asia included in the Peutinger Map.

title: Pons Aurelius
name_variants: Pons Aurelius@la | Pons Aurelius
description: The Pons Aurelius is known only from late Roman documents (fourth and fifth centuries CE) and is most likely the same bridge known as pons Antoninus in the early Middle Ages. The present-day Ponte Sisto (built in the fifteenth century) reused some of the ancient Roman bridge piers.

title: Pisuertes
name_variants: Pisuertes@la | Pisuertes
description: An ancient people of Umbria whose territory is now unlocated.

title: oppidum Noeta
name_variants: oppidum Noeta@la | oppidum Noeta
description: Pliny the Elder mentions the oppidum Noeta as part of his discussion of tribes in Iberia.

title: Via Clodia
name_variants: Via Clodia@la | Via Clodia
details: R. J. A. Talbert notes that the name 'Via Clodia" is included on the Tabula Peutingeriana on segment 4B4.
description: An ancient Roman road.

title: balneum Abascantis et Mamertini
name_variants: balneum Abascantis et Mamertini@la | balneum Abascantis et Mamertini
description: The balneum Abascanti were baths near the Porta Capena that were possibly built by T. Flavius Abascantus, the freedman of Domitian. Also near the Porta Capena were the balneum Mamertini, possibly dedicated by Sex. Petronius Mamertinus, praetorian prefect in 139-143 CE.

title: statua Valeriana
name_variants: statua Valeriana@la | statua Valeriana
description: A statue included in the Regionary Catalogue for Regio XIV, the Statua Valeriana evidently honored some members of the gens Valeria. It is possible that this statue in the Transtiberim replaced a bronze equestrian statue that depicted Cloelia or perhaps Valeria, the daughter of Valerius Poplicola, that had stood in summa Sacra Via until it was destroyed by fire prior to the time of Dionysius of Halicarnassus. Based on a Trajanic inscription (CIL 6, 975), the statue lent its name to a vicus.

title: Palatina
name_variants: Palatina@la | Palatina
details: The tribus Palatina was one of the four, large, urban tribes of Rome ( Palatina , Collina , Esquilina , Suburana ), which corresponded to the four urban regions that Servius Tullius created.
description: An urban tribe of Rome created under the reign of Servius Tullius.

title: Via Cornelia
name_variants: Via Cornelia@la | Via Cornelia
description: The Via Cornelia was an ancient road that ran along the north side of the circus Gai et Neronis. The road diverged from the Via Triumphalis west of the pons Neronianus, near a large tomb known as the Meta Romuli.

title: ad Catacumbas | memoria apostolorum
name_variants: ad Catacumbas@la | Catacombe di San Sebastiano@it | memoria apostolorum@la | ad Catacumbas | Catacombe di San Sebastiano | memoria apostolorum | ad Catacumbas | memoria apostolorum
description: The catacombs of San Sebastiano located on the Via Appia are located near the church of the same name. These hypogeal tombs emerged in the third century CE and were linked initially to the relics of the apostles Peter and Paul.

title: Fines exercitvs syriatic(a)e et conmertivm Barbaror(vm)
title_ipa: fines ekserkitvs siriatikae et konmertivm barbarorvm
name_variants: Fines exercitvs syriatic(a)e et conmertivm Barbaror(vm)@la | Fines exercitus Syriatice et conmertium Barbarorum | Fines exercitvs syriatic(a)e et conmertivm Barbaror(vm)
description: An area of the Syrian desert marked on the Peutinger Table that may indicate the boundary between the Roman province of Syria and a client state, possibly Palmyra.

title: promunturium Themisteas
name_variants: promunturium Themisteas@la | promunturium Themisteas | Themisteas (promuntorium) | promunturium Themisteas
description: Pliny the Elder describes Cape Themisteas as lying near the boundary of Farsistan and Elymais.

title: Voran
name_variants: Voran@la | Doune@en | Voran | Doune | Voran
description: A Roman fort of Flavian date located near modern Stirling, Scotland under and around the Doune Primary School. The Latin name "Voran", preserved in the Ravenna Cosmography, may be identifiable with this site. The fortifications seem to have been demolished and abandoned in the Roman era. Slight evidence (postholes) of possible prehistoric date have also been identified.

title: Victuriaci castri
name_variants: Victuriaci castri@la | Victuriacus | Victuriaci castri
description: A fortified place mentioned in Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks AD 532

title: Luceres
name_variants: Luceres@la | Luceres
description: An early Roman tribe from the time of Romulus.

title: Graero
name_variants: Graero@la | Graero
description: A name included on the Peutinger map. The "Graaei" were a Paeonian tribe whose territory was located on the Strymon River. Scholars debate whether this name should be correlated with the archaeological site of Terpni/Nigrita, a place located 21 kilometers southeast of Kalokastro.

title: Nautaca
name_variants: Keşş@ota | Kish@en | Kesh@en | Ναύτακα@grc | Nautaca@la | Keşş | Kish | Kesh | Nautaka | Nautaca | Nautaca
description: A large oasis settlement north of modern Shahrisabz in Uzbekistan that included the fortress of Uzunqïr. It is thought to be the location of ancient Kish/Kesh and possibly the Nautaka mentioned in Hellenistic Greco-Roman sources.

title: Regio X
name_variants: Regio X@la | Regio X
description: One of the administrative regions from Augustus's division of Italy, comprising Venetia and Histria. Described by Pliny the Elder in Book III of his Natural History.

title: Collis Uiminalis
name_variants: Collis Uiminalis@la | Monte Viminale@it | Collis Viminalis | Monte Viminale | Collis Uiminalis
description: The Viminal Hill, located between the Quirinal and Esquiline hills, is the smallest of the so-called seven hills of Rome.

title: Tullianum
name_variants: Carcere Mamertino@it | Mamertine Prison@en | Tullianum@la | Carcere Mamertino | Mamertine Prison | Tullianum | Tullianum
description: Prison located at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, named either for Servius Tullius (578–535 BCE) or for the spring (tullus) on which it was constructed. Also known as the Mamertine Prison. The church of San Giuseppe dei Falegnami was constructed on the site in the 11th century CE.

title: Crypta Balbi
name_variants: Crypta Balbi@la | Crypta Balbi
description: The Crypta Balbi, mentioned by name only in the Regionary Catalogues, most likely refers to a vaulted passageway built in the Campus Martius by the proconsul Lucius Cornelius Balbus in 15 BC, who also dedicated a theater there in the same year.

title: Fundus Albianus
name_variants: Fundus Albianus@la | Fundus Albianus
description: An estate located in the Pagus Ambitrebius mentioned on the Tabula alimentaria Traianea.

title: Surrentium
name_variants: Surrentium@la | Rhysadeiron@grc | Cap Ghir@fr | Surrentium | Rhysadeiron | Cap Ghir | Surrentium
details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Cap Ghir MOR
description: Present-day Cape Ghir, Morocco.

title: Porta Salaria
name_variants: Porta Salaria@la | Porta Salaria
description: A gate of the Aurelian Walls of Rome (ca. 271-275 CE) by means of which the Via Salaria exited the city, heading northward. The date was damaged during the bombardment of Rome in 1870 and was subsequently replaced (1873). The replacement gate was demolished in 1921. The site of the Porta Salaria is today occupied by Piazza Fiume.

title: Loretum | Lauretum
name_variants: Loretum@la | Lauretum@la | Loretum | Lauretum
description: A grove on the Aventine Hill in Rome, where it was claimed the tomb of Titus Tatius was once to be found.

title: Atabuli
name_variants: Atabuli@la | Atabuli
description: A tribe of ancient Ethiopia mentioned by Pliny the Elder as occupying lands beyond Egypt. Their territory likely lies between Napata and Meroë.

title: Hostra
name_variants: Hostra@la | Hostra
description: A place included on the Peutinger map, located along the route from Edessa to Tharrana.

title: Horti Largiani
name_variants: Horti Largiani@la | Horti Largiani
description: Gardens that were located in regio VII, but whose precise location is uncertain. They could have been in the Campus Martius or on the slopes of the Pincian Hill.

title: Sepulcra Salaria
name_variants: Sepolcreto salario@it | Sepulcra Salaria@la | Sepolcreto salario | Sepulcra Salaria | Sepulcra Salaria
description: The area known as "Sepulcra Salaria" corresponds to the current-day Piazza Fiume, a public square adjacent to the intersection of the Corso d'Italia and Via Piave. Beginning in the later republican period, this funereal area developed. A range of tomb typologies has been identified here.

title: Via Valeria
name_variants: Οὐαλερία ὁδός@grc | Via Valeria@la | Oualeria hodos | Oúalería hodós | Via Valeria | Via Valeria
description: An ancient road from Rome to Corfinium.

title: Canaria
name_variants: Canaria@la | Gran Canaria@es | Canaria | Gran Canaria | Canaria
details: The Barrington Atlas Directory notes: Gran Canaria
description: Canaria? (Gran Canaria) is an island of the Canary Islands archipelago.

title: Voltinia tribus
name_variants: Voltinia tribus@la | Voltinia tribus
details: The territory of the tribus Voltinia may be indicated by an imperial inscription, which lists the number of men who received free grain. Its location might be found on the left bank of the river Tiber, above the tribus Voturia .
description: The tribus Voltinia (or Votinia) was an older rural tribe of ancient Rome.

title: Graecostasis
name_variants: Graecostasis@la | Graecostasis
description: The Graecostasis was located at the margin of the comitium in the Forum Romanum. It was a tribunal where foreign ambassadors would wait.

title: Aula Palatina
name_variants: Konstantinbasilika@de | Aula Palatina@la | Basilica of Constantine@en | Konstantinbasilika | Aula Palatina | Basilica of Constantine | Aula Palatina
details: The basilica today houses the Church of the Redeemer. It is the largest extant hall from antiquity measuring 67 x 26.05 m, with a height of 33 m. The building was substantially damaged during World War II and restored afterwards.
description: The Aula Palatina is a Roman Imperial Basilica of the emperor Constantine (German: Konstantinbasilika) located at Trier, Germany. It was built ca. A.D. 310 as part of a Roman palace complex.

title: Marningum
name_variants: Mehring@de | Marningum@la | Mehring | Marningum | Marningum
description: Roman villa rustica in Mehring

title: Cylarabim gymnasium
name_variants: Κυλλαράβιον@grc | γυμνασίῳ τῷ Κυλαράβου@akk | Cylarabim gymnasium@la | Cyllarabion | Gymnasio to Kylarabon | Cylarabim gymnasium | Cylarabim gymnasium
description: A gymnasium built just outside of the walls of Argos. Now destroyed; its precise ancient location is unknown.

title: Columna Traiana
name_variants: Column of Trajan@en | Colonna Traiana@it | Trajanssäule (Die)@de | Columna Traiana@la | Säule des Traianus@de | Column of Trajan | Colonna Traiana | Trajanssaule | Columna Traiana | Säule des Traianus | Columna Traiana
description: The Column of Trajan (or Trajan's Column) is a victory column that was erected in the Forum of Trajan at Rome ca. 113 in order to commemorate Trajan's victories in the Dacian Wars. The column is particularly noted for its helical historiated bas relief frieze decoration.

title: Via Postumia
name_variants: Via Postumia@la | Via Postumia
description: A Roman road (via publica) of northern Italy begun in 148 B.C. by Spurius Postumius Albinus Magnus.

title: Horti Lamiani
name_variants: Horti Lamiani@la | Lamian Gardens@en | Horti Lamiani | Lamian Gardens | Horti Lamiani
description: Gardens on the Esquiline Hill that passed into the control of the Iulio-Claudian family from the consul Lucius Aelius Lamia. As imperial property, the gardens were adorned with opulent display architecture and sculpture.

title: Atrium Vestae
name_variants: House of the Vestals@en | Atrium Vestae@la | House of the Vestals | Atrium Vestae | Atrium Vestae

title: curiā Iulia
name_variants: curiā Iulia@la | Curia Julia@en | Curia Iulia | Curia Julia | curiā Iulia
details: Julius Caesar commissioned t he Curia Julia as a replacement for the earlier Curia Hostilia. The old Senate House was supposedly built by Tullus Hostilius. The building needed repairs after some of the furniture was used for the funeral pyre of Publius Clodius Pulcher in 52 BCE. The senate commissioned Faustus, the son of Sulla, to rebuild the building, which he did. However, when Julius Caesar came to power, he wanted to rebuild the Senate House as part of his Forum Iulium project. It is possible that Caesar was trying to rival Pompey, who had recently built a theatre. The Senate building, however, was not completed before his death. His adopted son Octavian, who would later become the emperor Augustus, took on the initiative to complete the senate house begun by Caesar. The house was finished in 29 BCE. The Curia Julia remained relatively the same and served its purpose as a meetinghouse until 283 CE. There was a fire that damaged the building, thus requiring repair. Diocletian repaired the curia in 303, and it is the one that still stands today. In 630 CE, the senate house was converted to a Christian church, and Pope Honorius I renamed it the Church of St. Adriano. It is this conversion to a church that has allowed the building to be so well preserved. Instead of being destroyed like other pagan symbols, it was protected. The exterior of the Curia Julia featured brick-faced concrete with a huge buttress at each angle. The lower part of the front wall was decorated with slabs of marble. The upper part was covered with stucco imitation of white marble blocks. A single flight of stairs led up to the bronze doors. The current bronze doors are modern replicas because the original bronze doors were transferred to the Basilica of St. John Lateran by Pope Alexander III in 1660. There was a small stoa, the Chalcidium, in front of the Curia that housed a statue of the goddess Minerva. A winged Victoria sat atop the crest of the rooftop. Minerva and Victoria represented both the wisdom of the senators and the power of the empire. In the assembly hall, there was seating for about three hundred senators, which was only half the Senate at that time. Originally, the walls of the room were decorated with colored marble, mosaics, and stucco work, and the wooden roof was gilded. In the back of the hall, there were seats for the consuls and the emperor. There was a depiction of Victoria that appeared to be descending upon the emperor The Senate House played an important function in Roman government, and the religious aspects of Roman Society can be seen in its use. In its first iteration as the Curia Hostilia, built at the end of the fifth century BCE, it served as a meeting place for the original senate, the council of elders. It was bordered by two temples, one to Saturn and the other to Castor and Pollux. By the third century, the Curia Hostilia itself was dedicated to the gods. The dedication of the place of assembly was required for the Senate to meet there. As the senate grew, it became necessary to enlarge the senate house to accommodate its numbers. It was also required that the people would be able to hear senatorial meetings, but non-senators were not allowed in the building itself, so it needed to be near an open area. Thus, the Senate house’s placement near the Forum was imperative. When the Curia Hostilia was burned down for Pulcher’s funeral pyre, Julius Caesar chose a slightly different placement for his Curia Julia, which was to overlook two forums: the Roman Forum and the Forum Iulium, which hadn’t been built yet. The gifting of a large and beautifully appointed building can be seen as a token nod to the prestige of the senate, indicating that they still had some power even after the republic. As Pontifex Maximus, Augustus was able to dedicate the building to the gods himself after construction was complete. Thus, even the meeting place of the senate was beholden to the powers of the principate, though not overtly.
